August has arrived at The Eye of Photography.

Send us your photos!

Until the end of August, you will find every morning a mix of world photographic news with your photos of the summer.

Gary Calderwood opens the month.

Anyone can send their summer image, but don’t forget that The Eye of Photography owes its survival essentially to its subscribers.

So, if you can, support us and subscribe.

Happy Summer !

Image 55: The Book Column: Here, they say the earth is ‘in love’ when it sticks to your boots. It observes the actions through which a landscape is shaped and the way in which bodies transform their environment just as much as they are transformed by it. For nearly three years, Rebekka Deubner returned to the Marais Poitevin almost every month, documenting the daily lives of market gardeners, livestock farmers and campaigners. A book published by Rotolux Press. An exhibition featured in the programme for the Rencontres d’Arles 2026. @rebekkadeubner @rotoluxpress @rencontresarles A column by @zoe.idb Photo: Rebekka Deubner, Mains de maraîcher et manifestant à Saint-Soline 2 lors des semis, 2023, série la terre amoureuse (se dit de la terre qui colle aux bottes), 2023-2026. Elle observe les gestes par lesquels un paysage est façonné et la manière dont les corps transforment leur environnement autant qu’ils sont transformés par lui. Pendant près de trois ans, Rebekka Deubner revient presque chaque mois dans le Marais poitevin, suivant le quotidien de maraîchers, d’éleveurs et de militants. Un livre publié chez Rotolux Press. A sailor smoking his pipe in the port of Naples. An elderly man with a sunburnt belly spilling over a red Speedo on a Greek beach… These missed photographs perhaps reveal her deepest obsession: capturing those fleeting moments that vanish before they are fully seen.” @mavrospictures A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Palma © Alexandra Mavros - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Le Questionnaire : « Alexandra Mavros photographie autant les images qu’elle réalise que celles qu’elle manque. Image 63: Our Week Favorite: Marie Mons embarks on a kind of quest for identity in this photographic series, in which she once again explores the theme of the self-portrait. Throughout, she consistently questions appearances: those of her body, those of her own gaze, and those of our own… A reciprocal exchange of questions between the subject, the artist and the viewer, oscillating between certainties (what Marie knows about herself) and discoveries (what the final image might reveal by capturing what eludes us). Marie Mons, ‘Self-Portraits’, published in the journals of the Maison François Méchain @mariemons @lamaisonfrancoismechain Photo: © Marie Mons - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : Marie Mons poursuit une forme de quête d’identité dans cette série photographique où elle creuse à nouveau la question de l’autoportrait. Avec constance, elle y interroge les apparences : celles de son corps, celles de son propre regard, celles du nôtre… Réciprocité des questions entre le modèle, l’artiste et le spectateur, va et vient entre certitudes (ce que Marie sait d’elle-même) et découvertes (ce que l’image finale pourrait révèler en captant ce qui échappe). Marie Mons, 'Autoportraits', publié dans les cahiers de la Maison François Méchain:

Image 65: Exhibition: Earlie Hudnall has been photographing Houston’s Third and Fourth Wards since the 1970s. These neighbourhoods have a fascinating African-American history; the Fourth Ward was founded by former freed slaves. Earlie has captured iconic images of Houston’s residents and has enjoyed a long and successful career, with his photographs featured in museum collections across the country. On view in the exhibition ‘From Sea To Shining Sea’ at the PDNB Gallery. @pdnbgallery Photo: Earlie Hudnall, Jr., Jumping Rope, 1997, Courtesy of PDNB Gallery, Denton, TX — — — — — Exposition : Earlie Hudnall photographie les Third et Fourth Wards de Houston depuis les années 1970. Ces quartiers possèdent une histoire afro-américaine passionnante ; le Fourth Ward a été fondé par d’anciens esclaves affranchis. Earlie a saisi des images emblématiques des habitants de Houston et a connu une carrière longue et fructueuse, ses photographies figurant dans des collections de musées à travers tout le pays. A voir dans l'exposition 'From Sea To Shining Sea' à la PDNB Gallery.

Image 67: Biennale: In a landscape where major photography events are often concentrated in large cities, the Xavier Miserachs Photography Biennale champions a different vision of a festival: an event on a human scale that fosters a dialogue between local memory and contemporary issues. And among the Biennale’s many highlights is ‘Travailleurs de la mer’ by Carles Palacio, which focuses on the fishermen of the Costa Brava and the vulnerabilities of a profession under threat. @carlespalacio @biennalxmiserachs Photo: Serie Trabajadores del Mar, Costa Brava, 2018-2022 - Carles Palacio — — — — — Biennale : Dans un paysage où les grands rendez-vous de l’image restent souvent concentrés dans les grandes villes, la Biennale de photographie Xavier Miserachs défend une autre idée du festival ; une manifestation à taille humaine capable de faire dialoguer mémoire locale et enjeux actuels. Et parmi les nombreux points forts de la Biennale, « Travailleurs de la mer » de Carles Palacio, consacré aux pêcheurs de la Costa Brava et aux fragilités d’un métier menacé.

Image 69: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. I work experimentally with processes such as projection, cyanotype, fabric and layered photographic techniques, creating intimate and reflective pieces grounded in lived experience.' — Sianna Campbell at Travel Through Art Studio. sianacampbell @travelthroughartstudio Photo: © Sianna Campbell — — — — Exposition : « Ma pratique s'articule autour de l'identité, de l'expérience émotionnelle et des espaces psychologiques dans lesquels évoluent les jeunes. Je recourt à la création d'images pour exprimer ce qui est souvent ressenti mais difficilement formulé. Je travaille de manière expérimentale avec des procédés tels que la projection, le cyanotype, le tissu et les techniques photographiques en superposition, afin de créer des œuvres intimes et propices à la réflexion, ancrées dans l'expérience vécue. » — Sianna Campbell, au Travel Through Art Studio. #siennacampbell #traveltroughartstudio

Image 75: Portfolio: ‘The rise of modern medicine has helped to postpone death in time, but has also shifted it in space. This paradigm shift means that, nowadays, the majority of our fellow citizens die in a healthcare setting. In the space of a few generations, what had been handed down since the beginning of time has become a fleeting art.’ Morgan Roué and his series ‘On the Banks of the Styx’. @carcinome Photo: Sur les rives du Styx © Morgan Roué — — — — — Portfolio : « L’essor de la médecine moderne a contribué à repousser la mort dans le temps, mais l’a aussi déplacé dans l’espace. Ce changement de paradigme implique qu’actuellement la majorité de nos concitoyens décèdent dans une structure de soins. En quelques générations, ce qui avait été hérité depuis le commencement est devenu un art évanescent ». Morgan Roué et sa série 'Sur les rives du Styx'.

Image 77: Exhibition: Emile Zola was also a photographer! Towards the end of his life, the writer developed a passion for photography and took several hundred photographs. Family portraits, landscapes, scenes from everyday life and compositions all reflect his flair for framing and lighting. The presence of the river and the outdoor scenes resonate with the setting at Croisset. @rmm_rouen Photo: Jacques Zola à bicyclette, entre Denise et Émile Zola, Verneuil-sur-Seine (Yvelines), d’après un négatif noir et blanc gélatino-argentique sur plaque de verre positivé, 6,5 x 9 cm, 1894-1902, Médiathèque du patrimoine et de la photographie (01K000490) © Ministère de la Culture, MPP, diff. GrandPalaisRmn Photo. — — — — — Exposition : Emile Zola était aussi photographe ! À la fin de sa vie, l’écrivain se passionne pour la photographie et réalise plusieurs centaines de clichés. Portraits de famille, paysages, scènes de vie et compositions traduisent son sens du cadrage et de la lumière. La présence du fleuve et les scènes en extérieur entrent en résonance avec le site de Croisset.

Image 81: Exhibition: From the period of Soviet censorship through the turbulent years of Ukraine’s independence, revolutions, and the onset of Russian military aggression, Kharkiv photographers have continuously expanded the boundaries of the medium, transforming it into a sharp instrument of social and aesthetic critique. According to their “punching theory”, a photograph should strike the viewer and disrupt habituai perception. 'Ukrainian Dreamers. The Kharkiv School Of Photography' is a large retrospective at the Radvila Palace Museum of Art, Vilnius, with Museum of the Kharkiv School of Photography, Kharkiv, Ukraine. @radvilurumai @moksop_museum @galerie_alexandra_de_viveiros Photo: Sergiy Solonsky, Untitiled, Bestiary series, 1995 — — — — — Exposition : De l’époque de la censure soviétique jusqu’aux années tumultueuses de l’indépendance de l’Ukraine, en passant par les révolutions et le début de l’agression militaire russe, les photographes de Kharkiv n’ont cessé de repousser les limites de ce médium, le transformant en un outil incisif de critique sociale et esthétique. Selon leur « théorie du coup de poing », une photographie doit frapper le spectateur et bouleverser sa perception habituelle. « Ukrainian Dreamers. L'école de photographie de Kharkiv » est une grande rétrospective au Musée d'art du palais Radvila, à Vilnius. #kharkivschool

Image 83: Portfolio: 'Lilac at Forty Four' is a photographic cycle of 20 images created in my studio at number 44 on a historic street in Łódź, Poland. At the emotional center of the series is the lilac, received as a gift from someone important: a symbol of spring and blooming, but also of loss and separation. Like Marcela Paniak, send us your portfolio at info@loeildelaphotographie.com @marcelapaniak Photo: © Marcela Paniak — — — — — Portfolio : « Le Lilas au quarante-quatre » est un cycle photographique de 20 images réalisé dans mon atelier situé au numéro 44 d’une rue historique de Łódź, en Pologne. Au centre émotionnel de la série se trouve le lilas, reçu en cadeau d’une personne importante : symbole du printemps et de l’épanouissement, mais aussi de la perte et de la séparation. Comme Marcela Paniak, envoyez-nous vos portfolios à info@loeildelaphotographie.com #marcelapaniak #portfolio

Published by MW Editions, this new photobook by the lens-based artist Susan kae Grant is a haunting collection of whimsical dreamscapes—(re)constructed from her childhood memories and dream explorations, carried out at home and in a lab.

Divided into seven chapters,Night Journey comprises some 90 black-and-white photographs taken—or, the way Grant puts it, made—over the past two and a half decades, starting in 2000.

Except for just a handful of triptychs, with side panels shot on location in Europe, all images in Night Journey were meticulously staged by Grant in her studio. Here, she acts as a shadow theater director orchestrating scenes that are devoid of color and evocative of fairy tales, nightmares, and—probably—Plato’s allegory of the cave.

In some cases, it takes Grant months to create her tableaux as she builds intricate sets, adding and removing layers of props, instructs models, and repositions lighting. The result of all this artistic effort is dreamlike shadow narratives that exist only in imagination, within the photograph.

Within the book, photographs interplay in more ways than just being paired across spreads; some form intriguing longer storylines—triptychs hidden inside foldouts or overlapping images printed on translucent paper.

“In the lush blacks and milky grays that saturate these pages, Grant materializes ghostly figures, animals, objects, and sometimes woods to get lost in. She invites us into a cumulative, immersive parallel existence of forms both absent and present.”

—Trudy Wilner Stack, writer and independent curator

Night Journey sprouted from Grant’s fascination with dreams and the unconscious. First, she wrote down, sketched or committed to tape her dreams—right after waking up in her bed. Next, she enlisted a sleep researcher, Dr. John Herman at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. In his lab, Grant was awakened from REM sleep to record her descriptions of the dream space.

These explorations led to a decades-long artistic endeavor that—using shadow as a metaphor—provides a pictorial access to the unconscious. The project has been displayed through the years at a series of solo exhibitions and will culminate in a retrospective show and this book.

“My interest in the shadow lies in the notion that nothing is certain except the opportunity to imagine and create conjecture. Today, as an artist, my quest is to channel enigmatic aspects of life.” —Susan kae Grant

Susan kae Grantis a lens-based artist, educator, and early creator and curator of photographic book arts. Her studio practice and distinct personal vision are recognized as significant contributions to the history of fabricated photography. Her work is held in major museums and private collections, including the J. Paul Getty Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. Professor of Art Emerita at Texas Woman’s University, she is represented by Conduit Gallery.

Origini Edizioni publishes Pâle by Gabrielle Duplantier.

This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory.

Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic.

The black notebook symbolizes imagination, thought, writing, a place for ideas: the working notebook is black par excellence, always and across all cultures.

Gabrielle Duplantier is a Franco-American-Azorean photographer born in 1978. She lives and works in Bayonne, France. Gabrielle Duplantier studied fine arts and history of art in the university of Bordeaux.

Back then, photography, which she had practiced since a young age, was a mere pastime.

Once she got her diploma, she decided to become independent and settled in Paris, where she worked as a photographer’s assistant or as a set photographer. Parallel to her many collaborations with the press, publishers or musicians, Gabrielle Duplantier pursued her personal work on the female portrait, one of her favourite topics. Another source of inspiration is Portugal, her home country, which she visits on a regular basis.

Gabrielle Duplantier :**Pâle

Origini Edizioni**Photos by Gabrielle Duplantier

Editing by Ilias Georgiadis and Gabrielle Duplantier Book design by Matilde Vittoria Laricchia Handcrafted work by Eugenia Koval

Dimensions: 21×29,7 cm

Paper: Favini Biancoflash Ivory 85 gr

50 photos, b/w

Language: French and English 500 numbered copies

Available at www.originiedizioni.com and selected retailers.

Image 55: The Book Column: Here, they say the earth is ‘in love’ when it sticks to your boots. It observes the actions through which a landscape is shaped and the way in which bodies transform their environment just as much as they are transformed by it. For nearly three years, Rebekka Deubner returned to the Marais Poitevin almost every month, documenting the daily lives of market gardeners, livestock farmers and campaigners. A book published by Rotolux Press. An exhibition featured in the programme for the Rencontres d’Arles 2026. @rebekkadeubner @rotoluxpress @rencontresarles A column by @zoe.idb Photo: Rebekka Deubner, Mains de maraîcher et manifestant à Saint-Soline 2 lors des semis, 2023, série la terre amoureuse (se dit de la terre qui colle aux bottes), 2023-2026. Avec l’aimable autorisation de l’artiste. — — — — — La Chronique Livre : Ici, on dit que la terre est « amoureuse » lorsqu’elle colle aux bottes. Elle observe les gestes par lesquels un paysage est façonné et la manière dont les corps transforment leur environnement autant qu’ils sont transformés par lui. Pendant près de trois ans, Rebekka Deubner revient presque chaque mois dans le Marais poitevin, suivant le quotidien de maraîchers, d’éleveurs et de militants. Un livre publié chez Rotolux Press. Une exposition au programme des Rencontres d'Arles 2026. #rebekkadeubner #thebookcolumn #photobook #zoeisledebeauchaine

Image 63: Our Week Favorite: Marie Mons embarks on a kind of quest for identity in this photographic series, in which she once again explores the theme of the self-portrait. Throughout, she consistently questions appearances: those of her body, those of her own gaze, and those of our own… A reciprocal exchange of questions between the subject, the artist and the viewer, oscillating between certainties (what Marie knows about herself) and discoveries (what the final image might reveal by capturing what eludes us). Marie Mons, ‘Self-Portraits’, published in the journals of the Maison François Méchain @mariemons @lamaisonfrancoismechain Photo: © Marie Mons - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : Marie Mons poursuit une forme de quête d’identité dans cette série photographique où elle creuse à nouveau la question de l’autoportrait. Avec constance, elle y interroge les apparences : celles de son corps, celles de son propre regard, celles du nôtre… Réciprocité des questions entre le modèle, l’artiste et le spectateur, va et vient entre certitudes (ce que Marie sait d’elle-même) et découvertes (ce que l’image finale pourrait révèler en captant ce qui échappe). Marie Mons, 'Autoportraits', publié dans les cahiers de la Maison François Méchain:

Image 65: Exhibition: Earlie Hudnall has been photographing Houston’s Third and Fourth Wards since the 1970s. These neighbourhoods have a fascinating African-American history; the Fourth Ward was founded by former freed slaves. Earlie has captured iconic images of Houston’s residents and has enjoyed a long and successful career, with his photographs featured in museum collections across the country. On view in the exhibition ‘From Sea To Shining Sea’ at the PDNB Gallery. @pdnbgallery Photo: Earlie Hudnall, Jr., Jumping Rope, 1997, Courtesy of PDNB Gallery, Denton, TX — — — — — Exposition : Earlie Hudnall photographie les Third et Fourth Wards de Houston depuis les années 1970. Ces quartiers possèdent une histoire afro-américaine passionnante ; le Fourth Ward a été fondé par d’anciens esclaves affranchis. Earlie a saisi des images emblématiques des habitants de Houston et a connu une carrière longue et fructueuse, ses photographies figurant dans des collections de musées à travers tout le pays. A voir dans l'exposition 'From Sea To Shining Sea' à la PDNB Gallery.

Image 67: Biennale: In a landscape where major photography events are often concentrated in large cities, the Xavier Miserachs Photography Biennale champions a different vision of a festival: an event on a human scale that fosters a dialogue between local memory and contemporary issues. And among the Biennale’s many highlights is ‘Travailleurs de la mer’ by Carles Palacio, which focuses on the fishermen of the Costa Brava and the vulnerabilities of a profession under threat. @carlespalacio @biennalxmiserachs Photo: Serie Trabajadores del Mar, Costa Brava, 2018-2022 - Carles Palacio — — — — — Biennale : Dans un paysage où les grands rendez-vous de l’image restent souvent concentrés dans les grandes villes, la Biennale de photographie Xavier Miserachs défend une autre idée du festival ; une manifestation à taille humaine capable de faire dialoguer mémoire locale et enjeux actuels. Et parmi les nombreux points forts de la Biennale, « Travailleurs de la mer » de Carles Palacio, consacré aux pêcheurs de la Costa Brava et aux fragilités d’un métier menacé.

Image 69: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. I work experimentally with processes such as projection, cyanotype, fabric and layered photographic techniques, creating intimate and reflective pieces grounded in lived experience.' — Sianna Campbell at Travel Through Art Studio. sianacampbell @travelthroughartstudio Photo: © Sianna Campbell — — — — Exposition : « Ma pratique s'articule autour de l'identité, de l'expérience émotionnelle et des espaces psychologiques dans lesquels évoluent les jeunes. Je recourt à la création d'images pour exprimer ce qui est souvent ressenti mais difficilement formulé. The exhibition is called: The Teenage Self.It brings together 2 photographers: Sarah Lee Lewis and Iain McKell.

It is the latter that we have chosen to present to you.

He gave us this text!

Private Reality– A Diary of a Teenage Boy

In 1976 aged nineteen while studying at Exeter College of Art I got my self a summer job on Weymouth seafront photographing holiday makers. I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to earn a living but at the same time doing a personal project showing the life of the sea side photographer.

Its about youth culture and being a teenager in the 70’s. Existential angst was preoccupying my thoughts.

It all came together through the lens as I was turning from a teenager to a young adult.

As well as the holiday makers I was photographing local people from the town, my friends, family and into the evening with the disco bars fair grounds and caravan parks.

I was also experimenting with abstraction through the graphic nature of photography.

It was my right of passage and coming of age and I started to look at the world through the camera.

The Cars – Sea View series

I saw these people in there cars, It’s a very British thing to do to drive to the sea side and (most probably because of the bad weather too) not actually get out the car but sea view gaze from with in that window. Its a bit like a camera you’re in a box looking out detached from the world taking in your experience.

So that observation and the inherent interest in my world around me along with my sense of humour and it was 1976 the year Punk hit the tabloids and Johny Rotten swearing on TV, youth culture was spitting at every one and doing V up with there fingers `I was a bit of a punk more in attitude than dress but it was I thought a bit ‘Catcher in the Rye’ by J. D. Salinger(a quote from google) ‘adolescents for its themes of angst, alienation, and as a critique of superficiality in society’ My friends at the time loved t˙is book I had the balls just to confront the people in there boxes and photograph them in the name of free speech and being rebellious, seeing the irony and humour and how they were maybe trapped in there cars and there lives. By doing this I was catching there unguarded reactions to what I was doing like utter surprise or confusion on their faces. I think it was punky a bit passive aggressive but harmless. Although the women you see getting out her car with the glamorous sun glasses and partner smiling came towards me and started hitting me with her hand bag saying ‘You can’t just go around photographing people without asking them’ but off course you can in a public space. I think I was like Ringo in Hard Day Night Beatles movie. Maybe I was escaping my reality rather than confronting it or its both.

Iain McKell

Von Lintel Gallery presents “The Surfing Landscape”. This multimedia exhibit pairs large-scale tintypes, prints, and a new film by photographer Joni Sternbach. This is the gallery’s third solo exhibition with the artist.

Joni Sternbach is renowned for her use of the wet plate collodion process, an early photographic technique dating back to the 19th century, in which a metal plate is coated with a silver salt solution, exposed in a large-format camera, and developed in a portable darkroom on the spot to produce an instant positive photograph, like the 1850’s version of a Polaroid. Sternbach is a master of this complex process, and the incredible clarity and size of her tintypes demonstrate her skill.

Sternbach’s use of the tintype process works on many levels; it fosters the collaboration between her and her subjects and brings people together. The images possess a unique and timeless quality, which resonates with the rich history of surfing and its enduring appeal. Although not originally her goal, Sternbach quickly became fascinated with the surfers who she first saw as obstacles to her shots of the ocean. She has been following them and their practice all over the world since then.

“The Surfing Landscape” features an assortment of Sternbach’s rarely seen mammoth works (14×17 and 16×20 inches). There will also be a selection of her complex, multi-panel tintypes (10×20 and 14×33 inches). These large-scale tintype portraits of surfers capture the rugged and raw beauty of their athleticism, and the spirit of adventure that drives them. The images are powerful and evocative, and much like the historical process that Sternbach uses, her photographs evoke a timelessness that transports the viewer.

This exhibition also features Sternbach’s film entitled “Making Pictures”, a two-channel, experimental piece about her experience making wet plate collodion tintypes in the field. Shot with a Go-Pro camera strapped to her tripod leg, this nine minute film is presented as a meditation about process, people, time, and space. Inspired by the transcendental film movement, it takes its cues from Sternbach’s own slow style of photography.

Sternbach is a native New Yorker. She received a BFA in Photography from the School of Visual Arts and an MA from New York University/International Center of Photography. Her work is held in many public collections including the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the National Portrait Gallery in London, the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, and the Peabody Essex Museum, among others.

Alexandra Mavros : The art of photographing hat slips away

In the work of Alexandra Mavros, an image rarely emerges where you’d expect. It is not built around the decisive moment, but around what comes just before or just after it, in those fleeting fractions of a second when reality momentarily stops performing its own role. Perhaps this is where the singularity of her gaze lies: photographing not the event itself, but its release. A Paris-based photographer and filmmaker of Greek-Canadian heritage, Alexandra Mavros has developed a practice shaped as much by cinema as by photography. The “fourth wall,” a notion she readily embraces, is more than a cinematic reference it is a way of seeing. Her lens is instinctively drawn to what happens behind the scenes: involuntary gestures, distracted glances, those subtle moments when the staging begins to crack and humanity quietly reclaims the image. Far removed from a fashion photography driven by visual demonstration, her work embraces accident, spontaneity, and observation. Soft, natural, cinematic light accompanies rather than dramatizes. Each photograph feels suspended, like a story deliberately left unfinished, inviting the viewer to imagine what lies beyond the frame. This search for a beauty inseparable from truth an acknowledged legacy of Peter Lindbergh is enriched by a discreet irony that recalls both Martin Parr and Elliott Erwitt. Her humor is never demonstrative; it emerges through details, unexpected juxtapositions, and coincidences that only a patient eye can perceive. Reading this Questionnaire, one thing becomes immediately apparent: Alexandra Mavros is as fascinated by the photographs she never took as by those she did. A Chihuahua in a stroller on the Croisette. A sailor smoking his pipe in the port of Naples. An elderly man with a sunburnt belly spilling over a red Speedo on a Greek beach… These missed photographs perhaps reveal her deepest obsession: capturing those fleeting moments that vanish before they are fully seen. At a time when algorithms increasingly standardize the way we look, Alexandra Mavros reminds us that “photographs are meant to be printed, touched, and leafed through not liked.” A simple statement that perfectly encapsulates her practice: attentive, demanding, and deeply committed to everything that escapes the relentless speed of contemporary images. For her, photography neither seeks to impress nor to prove; it simply waits for reality, however briefly, to forget that it is being watched.

Web Site:www.macrospictures.com

Instagram: @mavrospictures

What was your first photographic trigger?Alexandra Mavros: I was fifteen, holding my first camera, with my sister as my subject and my father by my side as my guide. He was teaching me how to master light, and to explain depth of field, he slipped his hand between my lens and my sister’s face. I pressed the shutter before he had time to move it away—and that was the real trigger. Photography suddenly allowed me to capture what the naked eye lets slip away: a hand moving too fast, a little sister who wasn’t grown up yet, and a moment no one else would have noticed.

Who is the image-maker who inspires you most?Alexandra Mavros: I’m terrible with first names—and even worse with making decisions. There’s Peter Lindbergh, to whom I devoted my thesis, especially his ability to unite beauty and truth. Then there’s Martin Parr and Elliott Erwitt, who are probably my favorite comedians. And Sayombhu Mukdeeprom, one of the first cinematographers whose vision made me look up his name in the end credits. I’ll stop there.

Which image do you wish you had made?Alexandra Mavros: Not one image, but a series: Lunchtime by Charles H. Traub. Candid portraits taken during lunch breaks in the 1970s. Color—and nerve!

Which image has moved you the most?Alexandra Mavros: A photograph of my mother when she was my age.

Which image has made you angry?Alexandra Mavros: Any image devoid of humanity.

A key image in your personal pantheon?Alexandra Mavros:Lovers. A tender kiss in front of the red-carpet barrier at the Cannes Film Festival. I pressed the shutter without breaking my stride I just happened to be there at the right moment. That photograph made me want to see my work printed large. I’d love to find those lovers one day and give them a print.

A photographic memory from your childhood?Alexandra Mavros: I was ten, armed with the family camcorder and pockets full of stories. I directed my sister and our cousins from England in our dining room. I dressed them, briefed them on their characters, and kept them acting until we couldn’t stop laughing. It’s one of my happiest memories. Twenty years later, I still haven’t stopped creating with my friends whether in a single frame or twenty-four frames per second.

The image that obsesses you?Alexandra Mavros: The one I didn’t dare to take. A Chihuahua in a stroller during the Cannes Film Festival. A sailor in uniform smoking his pipe in the port of Naples. An over-tanned octogenarian with his belly spilling out of a bright red Speedo on a Greek beach.

Which image changed the world?Alexandra Mavros: The one that came from the other side of the world.

Which image changed your world?Alexandra Mavros: The very first one I took with my grandfather’s old camera, then had developed in a lab.

If money were no object, which artwork would you dream of owning?Alexandra Mavros: My walls are covered with movie posters and family photographs. Once I have a blank wall, I’ll come back to that question.

In your opinion, what quality is essential to becoming a good photographer?Alexandra Mavros: Knowing how to let go and how to take the shot.

What is the secret of the perfect image, if such a thing exists?Alexandra Mavros: To make it. The Latin root of the word perfect, perficere, means “to complete, to bring to fulfillment.” A photograph that has been made is already a perfect photograph. And if I were allowed a second secret: synchronicity.

Who would you most like to photograph?Alexandra Mavros: Whoever is wearing colorful clothes.

Who would you most like to be photographed by?Alexandra Mavros: My grandfather.

An indispensable photography book?Alexandra Mavros: A Taschen book I bought at Paris Photo last year: the making-of of the first James Bond film, Dr. No. Cinema, photography, behind the scenes everything I love gathered into one object.

What was the camera of your childhood?Alexandra Mavros: The one on my first phone: a Sony Ericsson. The one I borrowed from my father: a Nikon F4. The one I eventually made my own: a Nikon D3100.

Which camera do you use today?Alexandra Mavros: A Sony A7 IV for its versatility. A Leica Q for traveling light. And a Canon Ixus 185 for the memories that end up in shared family albums.

Your favorite drug?Alexandra Mavros: Mastika.

How do you disconnect?Alexandra Mavros: Dancing with my friends in Irish pubs on Friday nights.

What question unsettles you the most?Alexandra Mavros: “How are you?”

What is your relationship with the image?Alexandra Mavros: Reciprocal.

Your greatest quality?Alexandra Mavros: Passing things on according to my astrologer.

Your latest act of madness?Alexandra Mavros: Joining a table tennis club in Le Marais.

An image to illustrate a new banknote?Alexandra Mavros: One of William Wegman’s Weimaraners.

A job you would never have wanted to do?Alexandra Mavros: One that wouldn’t let me do three others at the same time.

Your greatest professional extravagance?Alexandra Mavros: Printing on baryta paper.

Can photography change our collective perception of an event or an era?Alexandra Mavros: Absolutely. Photography can justify wars just as easily as it can end careers. But just as history books often distort or simply omit certain narratives, it is not photography itself that holds the power so much as the choice of what is shown and what is left unseen.

How do you perceive the influence of social media on the way photographs are created and perceived today?Alexandra Mavros: Like everything else, it’s a double-edged sword. As artists, we have more visibility and inspiration at our fingertips than ever before, but if we’re not careful, those very fingers can get cut off. We compose for the 4:5 ratio instead of the story we want to tell. We let the algorithm dictate our creativity, and when it doesn’t validate us, anxiety creeps in until we no longer want to post or even photograph. To avoid losing ourselves, we have to remember that the pleasure lies in the act itself, not in the “like.” Photographs are meant to be printed, touched, and leafed through not merely liked.

One Instagram account everyone should follow?Alexandra Mavros: @sciuraglam.

What’s the last thing you did for the first time?Alexandra Mavros: Getting out of bed on the right foot.

What makes a successful photograph?Alexandra Mavros: A photograph that has been taken.

What interests you most in an image?Alexandra Mavros: Recognition. Seeing something that feels true.

What distinguishes photography from art photography?Alexandra Mavros: The difference lies less in the photograph than in the wall it’s hung on. A picture of the tin of sardines I had for breakfast becomes art the moment I place a museum label next to it.

Which city, country, or culture do you dream of discovering?Alexandra Mavros: Brazil. Or Nepal. Or Indonesia. I’m not difficult I will happily go wherever someone is willing to host me.

A place you never tire of?Alexandra Mavros: Greece in the summer.

Your greatest regret?Alexandra Mavros: NO REGRETS.

Color or black and white?Alexandra Mavros: Color to attract. Black and white to undress.

Daylight or artificial light?Alexandra Mavros: Natural light until I discovered the flash gun.

In your opinion, what is the world’s most photogenic city?Alexandra Mavros: Sant’Angelo, Ischia. Full of color and elegantly dressed retirees.

If God existed, would you ask Him to pose for you, or would you rather take a selfie with Him?Alexandra Mavros: Neither. He’d probably be overexposed.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table?Alexandra Mavros: My mother, for love. Shams of Tabriz, for truth. Kate McKinnon, for laughter. Marco Bezzecchi, for the motorcycle ride after dessert. Howard Hawks, to film it all. And my friends, to complete the picture.

Which image best represents the current state of the world?Alexandra Mavros: The censored one.

If you had to start all over again?Alexandra Mavros: Less doubt, more momentum.

Last word?Alexandra Mavros: Gratitude.

MIA Photo Fair BNP Paribas will return to Milan from the 18th to the 21st of March 2027 at Superstudio Più, with a preview for collectors and the press on March 17th. Organised by Fiere di Parma and directed by Francesca Malgara for the fourth consecutive year, the fair will present its sixteenth edition.

The 2027 edition adopts Belonging as its central theme, following previous editions dedicated to Change, Dialogues and Metamorphosis. The programme will examine how photography addresses questions of identity, community and place in the context of contemporary social and cultural change.

According to the organisers, the concept of belonging extends beyond geographical origin to encompass relationships, shared experiences and collective memory. Photography is presented as a medium capable of documenting these connections while exploring the links between personal histories, communities and territories.

“With Belonging, we have chosen a word that resonates with many of the profound transformations shaping contemporary society,” says artistic director Francesca Malgara. “Photography is perhaps the medium best equipped to explore how we connect with people, places, communities, ideas and memories.”

The 2027 edition also introduces an updated curatorial structure. The Main Section will continue to bring together Italian and international galleries specialising in photography and lens-based practices.

The Beyond Photography – Dialogue | Work in Progress section will be curated by Rischa Paterlini, who previously oversaw the international FOCUS section. The programme will explore artistic practices that expand beyond traditional photographic formats, incorporating installation, moving image, archives and digital technologies. Participating galleries will present projects by artists from different generations whose work examines themes including identity, memory, landscape and belonging.

The Reportage Beyond Reportage section, curated by Emanuela Mazzonis di Pralafera, will continue to focus on contemporary documentary photography. Bringing together photographers from different generations and geographical contexts, it will present projects that move beyond conventional reportage towards more interpretative forms of visual storytelling.

Further announcements concerning the third curated section, participating galleries, invited guests, awards and the cultural programme will be made in the coming months.

**Applications for galleries are now open and will remain available until the 10th of December 2026, with an early application rate offered until October 20th.

Image 75: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. I work experimentally with processes such as projection, cyanotype, fabric and layered photographic techniques, creating intimate and reflective pieces grounded in lived experience.' — Sianna Campbell at Travel Through Art Studio. sianacampbell @travelthroughartstudio Photo: © Sianna Campbell — — — — Exposition : « Ma pratique s'articule autour de l'identité, de l'expérience émotionnelle et des espaces psychologiques dans lesquels évoluent les jeunes. Je recourt à la création d'images pour exprimer ce qui est souvent ressenti mais difficilement formulé. Je travaille de manière expérimentale avec des procédés tels que la projection, le cyanotype, le tissu et les techniques photographiques en superposition, afin de créer des œuvres intimes et propices à la réflexion, ancrées dans l'expérience vécue. » — Sianna Campbell, au Travel Through Art Studio. #siennacampbell #traveltroughartstudio

Image 81: Portfolio: ‘The rise of modern medicine has helped to postpone death in time, but has also shifted it in space. En quelques générations, ce qui avait été hérité depuis le commencement est devenu un art évanescent ». Morgan Roué et sa série 'Sur les rives du Styx'.

Image 83: Exhibition: Emile Zola was also a photographer! Towards the end of his life, the writer developed a passion for photography and took several hundred photographs. La présence du fleuve et les scènes en extérieur entrent en résonance avec le site de Croisset.

Image 87: Exhibition: From the period of Soviet censorship through the turbulent years of Ukraine’s independence, revolutions, and the onset of Russian military aggression, Kharkiv photographers have continuously expanded the boundaries of the medium, transforming it into a sharp instrument of social and aesthetic critique. According to their “punching theory”, a photograph should strike the viewer and disrupt habituai perception. 'Ukrainian Dreamers. The Kharkiv School Of Photography' is a large retrospective at the Radvila Palace Museum of Art, Vilnius, with Museum of the Kharkiv School of Photography, Kharkiv, Ukraine. @radvilurumai @moksop_museum @galerie_alexandra_de_viveiros Photo: Sergiy Solonsky, Untitiled, Bestiary series, 1995 — — — — — Exposition : De l’époque de la censure soviétique jusqu’aux années tumultueuses de l’indépendance de l’Ukraine, en passant par les révolutions et le début de l’agression militaire russe, les photographes de Kharkiv n’ont cessé de repousser les limites de ce médium, le transformant en un outil incisif de critique sociale et esthétique. Selon leur « théorie du coup de poing », une photographie doit frapper le spectateur et bouleverser sa perception habituelle. « Ukrainian Dreamers. L'école de photographie de Kharkiv » est une grande rétrospective au Musée d'art du palais Radvila, à Vilnius. #kharkivschool

Image 89: Portfolio: 'Lilac at Forty Four' is a photographic cycle of 20 images created in my studio at number 44 on a historic street in Łódź, Poland. At the emotional center of the series is the lilac, received as a gift from someone important: a symbol of spring and blooming, but also of loss and separation. Like Marcela Paniak, send us your portfolio at info@loeildelaphotographie.com @marcelapaniak Photo: © Marcela Paniak — — — — — Portfolio : « Le Lilas au quarante-quatre » est un cycle photographique de 20 images réalisé dans mon atelier situé au numéro 44 d’une rue historique de Łódź, en Pologne. Au centre émotionnel de la série se trouve le lilas, reçu en cadeau d’une personne importante : symbole du printemps et de l’épanouissement, mais aussi de la perte et de la séparation. Comme Marcela Paniak, envoyez-nous vos portfolios à info@loeildelaphotographie.com #marcelapaniak #portfolio

Selon leur « théorie du coup de poing », une photographie doit frapper le spectateur et bouleverser sa perception habituelle. « Ukrainian Dreamers. Because it is essential to support creativity and diversity of perspectives, the UPP is organising a free competition, with no set theme, aimed at supporting two professional photographers in the design and realisation of a photographic project. These grants are intended to help the winners bring their projects to fruition and present them at a joint exhibition to be held at the Maison des photographes, the UPP’s headquarters (Paris, 10th arrondissement).

Prizes: A grant of €4,000 for a photographer who is a member of the UPP and a grant of €2,000 for a photographer who is not a member.

Closing date: 6 September 2026

Eligibility criteria: These grants are open to professional photographers of legal age who are resident in France.

A book published by Rotolux Press. Image 67: Our Week Favorite: Marie Mons embarks on a kind of quest for identity in this photographic series, in which she once again explores the theme of the self-portrait. Throughout, she consistently questions appearances: those of her body, those of her own gaze, and those of our own… A reciprocal exchange of questions between the subject, the artist and the viewer, oscillating between certainties (what Marie knows about herself) and discoveries (what the final image might reveal by capturing what eludes us). Marie Mons, ‘Self-Portraits’, published in the journals of the Maison François Méchain @mariemons @lamaisonfrancoismechain Photo: © Marie Mons - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : Marie Mons poursuit une forme de quête d’identité dans cette série photographique où elle creuse à nouveau la question de l’autoportrait. Avec constance, elle y interroge les apparences : celles de son corps, celles de son propre regard, celles du nôtre… Réciprocité des questions entre le modèle, l’artiste et le spectateur, va et vient entre certitudes (ce que Marie sait d’elle-même) et découvertes (ce que l’image finale pourrait révèler en captant ce qui échappe). Marie Mons, 'Autoportraits', publié dans les cahiers de la Maison François Méchain:

Image 69: Exhibition: Earlie Hudnall has been photographing Houston’s Third and Fourth Wards since the 1970s. These neighbourhoods have a fascinating African-American history; the Fourth Ward was founded by former freed slaves. Earlie has captured iconic images of Houston’s residents and has enjoyed a long and successful career, with his photographs featured in museum collections across the country. On view in the exhibition ‘From Sea To Shining Sea’ at the PDNB Gallery. @pdnbgallery Photo: Earlie Hudnall, Jr., Jumping Rope, 1997, Courtesy of PDNB Gallery, Denton, TX — — — — — Exposition : Earlie Hudnall photographie les Third et Fourth Wards de Houston depuis les années 1970. Ces quartiers possèdent une histoire afro-américaine passionnante ; le Fourth Ward a été fondé par d’anciens esclaves affranchis. Earlie a saisi des images emblématiques des habitants de Houston et a connu une carrière longue et fructueuse, ses photographies figurant dans des collections de musées à travers tout le pays. A voir dans l'exposition 'From Sea To Shining Sea' à la PDNB Gallery.

Image 71: Biennale: In a landscape where major photography events are often concentrated in large cities, the Xavier Miserachs Photography Biennale champions a different vision of a festival: an event on a human scale that fosters a dialogue between local memory and contemporary issues. And among the Biennale’s many highlights is ‘Travailleurs de la mer’ by Carles Palacio, which focuses on the fishermen of the Costa Brava and the vulnerabilities of a profession under threat. @carlespalacio @biennalxmiserachs Photo: Serie Trabajadores del Mar, Costa Brava, 2018-2022 - Carles Palacio — — — — — Biennale : Dans un paysage où les grands rendez-vous de l’image restent souvent concentrés dans les grandes villes, la Biennale de photographie Xavier Miserachs défend une autre idée du festival ; une manifestation à taille humaine capable de faire dialoguer mémoire locale et enjeux actuels. Et parmi les nombreux points forts de la Biennale, « Travailleurs de la mer » de Carles Palacio, consacré aux pêcheurs de la Costa Brava et aux fragilités d’un métier menacé.

Image 73: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. I work experimentally with processes such as projection, cyanotype, fabric and layered photographic techniques, creating intimate and reflective pieces grounded in lived experience.' — Sianna Campbell at Travel Through Art Studio. sianacampbell @travelthroughartstudio Photo: © Sianna Campbell — — — — Exposition : « Ma pratique s'articule autour de l'identité, de l'expérience émotionnelle et des espaces psychologiques dans lesquels évoluent les jeunes. Je recourt à la création d'images pour exprimer ce qui est souvent ressenti mais difficilement formulé. Je travaille de manière expérimentale avec des procédés tels que la projection, le cyanotype, le tissu et les techniques photographiques en superposition, afin de créer des œuvres intimes et propices à la réflexion, ancrées dans l'expérience vécue. » — Sianna Campbell, au Travel Through Art Studio. #siennacampbell #traveltroughartstudio

Image 79: Portfolio: ‘The rise of modern medicine has helped to postpone death in time, but has also shifted it in space. This paradigm shift means that, nowadays, the majority of our fellow citizens die in a healthcare setting. In the space of a few generations, what had been handed down since the beginning of time has become a fleeting art.’ Morgan Roué and his series ‘On the Banks of the Styx’. @carcinome Photo: Sur les rives du Styx © Morgan Roué — — — — — Portfolio : « L’essor de la médecine moderne a contribué à repousser la mort dans le temps, mais l’a aussi déplacé dans l’espace. Ce changement de paradigme implique qu’actuellement la majorité de nos concitoyens décèdent dans une structure de soins. En quelques générations, ce qui avait été hérité depuis le commencement est devenu un art évanescent ». Morgan Roué et sa série 'Sur les rives du Styx'.

Image 81: Exhibition: Emile Zola was also a photographer! Towards the end of his life, the writer developed a passion for photography and took several hundred photographs. Family portraits, landscapes, scenes from everyday life and compositions all reflect his flair for framing and lighting. The presence of the river and the outdoor scenes resonate with the setting at Croisset. @rmm_rouen Photo: Jacques Zola à bicyclette, entre Denise et Émile Zola, Verneuil-sur-Seine (Yvelines), d’après un négatif noir et blanc gélatino-argentique sur plaque de verre positivé, 6,5 x 9 cm, 1894-1902, Médiathèque du patrimoine et de la photographie (01K000490) © Ministère de la Culture, MPP, diff. GrandPalaisRmn Photo. — — — — — Exposition : Emile Zola était aussi photographe ! À la fin de sa vie, l’écrivain se passionne pour la photographie et réalise plusieurs centaines de clichés. Portraits de famille, paysages, scènes de vie et compositions traduisent son sens du cadrage et de la lumière. La présence du fleuve et les scènes en extérieur entrent en résonance avec le site de Croisset.

Editorial RM presents SACA 1504, by Manuel Naranjo Martell: a photobook on an ancestral ritual that forms part of America’s equestrian roots.

Developed over nearly a decade around the Saca de las Yeguas — the annual roundup of mares — in Doñana, Huelva, southern Spain, a vast marshland comprising a National Park and Natural Park, and recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site and Biosphere Reserve, the book is conceived as a long-form work that brings together photography, historical research, and cultural reflection on the relationship between territory, horse, and memory.

The project takes as its starting point the ancestral practice of the Saca de las Yeguas, formally established in 1504 through an ordinance issued by the Duke of Medina Sidonia, although its roots go back to earlier livestock traditions linked to Al-Andalus and the historic management of the marshlands. Within this context, the photobook highlights the yegüerizos as essential bearers of a form of knowledge transmitted orally and through the body—deeply bound to both the horse and the landscape of Doñana.

SACA 1504 offers a visual reading of a shared historical and cultural heritage between the lower Guadalquivir region and the Americas, structured around a profound equestrian connection rooted both in the yegüerizos of Doñana and in the horse cultures of Native American peoples, the so-called Horse Nation.

“The marshland grips the feet of anyone who steps into it.” From this physical and symbolic experience, SACA 1504 emerges: from a deep bond with a specific landscape that, for Manuel Naranjo Martell, lies between his two inheritances – Spain and the United States – between Andalusian roots and their American resonance. This dual sense of belonging runs through the work and turns the photobook into an exploration of identity, heritage, and landscape as a living archive.

Format: 240 × 312 mm.

Binding: hard cover with printed cloth binding.

Typefaces: Quarto and Lyon.

Paper: Fedrigoni Freelife Vellum White 140 g; opening printed on Olin Design Regular Soft White 80 g.

End section: facsimile fold-out sheet.

www.manuelnaranjomartell.com

A two-day workshop with Christopher Morris, founding member of the VII Photo Agency.

For two days only, work side by side with one of the most influential documentary photographers of the last forty years. With four decades spent documenting contemporary history for TIME Magazine and the VII Photo Agency, Christopher Morris will share his approach, his creative process, and give you direct feedback on your own work.

Presented exclusively for Trieste Photo Days and limited to 15 participants.

What the two days include

1. Opening session. A two-hour introduction in which Morris shares his personal and professional journey and the ideas that have shaped his work.

2. Group portfolio reviews. Every participant’s work is reviewed with the whole group present, for open discussion and mutual learning.

3. Bring your work. Up to 60 images in a folder with your name, on laptop, SSD or hard drive. Prints and book dummies are welcome too.

Image 73: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. Refine Your Vision. Build Your Voice. Showcase Your Work.

ONLY TWO PLACES LEFT

The BOYS! BOYS! BOYS! Photo Course is designed for artists ready to elevate their practice, guiding you from an idea to a fully realised body of work – whether that’s an exhibition, a zine, or a published book.

Through mentorship, personalised assignments, and expert guidance, you’ll refine your visual language, strengthen your storytelling, and develop a project that is truly your own.

Personalised exercises will challenge you to push boundaries, think critically, and lay a strong foundation for your final project. You’ll explore research methods, conceptual development, and visual cohesion—all essential elements of a compelling photographic series.

Each month, experienced guest speakers will present their area of expertise, provide in-depth feedback, helping you refine your ideas. In the final stage of the program, you’ll present your project—whether as an exhibition, zine, or publication layout—for critique and final refinement.

This course is ideal for photographers eager to commit to their practice, push their creative limits, and develop a significant body of work with professional guidance.

Developing a photographic series with a clear artistic vision

Presenting your work for exhibitions and online platforms

Developing your unique visual language and artistic identity

Research, idea generation, and conceptual storytelling

Editing, sequencing, and incorporating text with imagery

Design, branding, and layout for publication

Sustainable creative business strategies

Course Structure & Sessions

6pm London

7pm Paris

5am Sydney (+1 day)

1pm New York

Session 1 – 5th September – Creative & Sustainable Business strategies and planning with Paul McDonald

Session 2 – 12th September – Storytelling & Creating a Visually Cohesive Narrative with Aletheia Casey.

Session 3 – 26th September – Design & Branding with Studio Kunz

Session 4 – 10th October – Printing & Presentation Techniques with Chau Digital

Session 5 – 24th October – Grant Applications, Writing & Pitching Yourself with Nigel Grimmer & Paul McDonald

Session 6 – 7th November – Presenting your work for exhibitions and Online with Ghislain Pascal and Paul McDonald

Session 7 – 21st November – Editing Techniques and Project Development with Aletheia Casey & Paul McDonald

Session 8 – 5th December – Final Presentation to Ghislain Pascal

The course is limited to only 8 people. All students must identify as queer or gay.

We offer a monthly payment plan so please contact us is you’d like to discuss your payment plan at boys@thelittleblackgallery.com

Please note the sessions will be delivered using zoom, the sessions will not be recorded. Students cannot record the sessions for copyright, privacy and confidentiality reasons of all involved.

Yancey Richardson announces Once More, With Feeling, a group exhibition highlighting the work of the 2026 Yale MFA graduates in photography: Christian Badach, Chen Xiangyun, Jasmine Clarke, Faith Couch, Christopher Postlewaite, Olivia Reavey, John Shen, Em Wall and Andrew Warner. A group artist walkthrough of the exhibition will be held on August 13th, from 3–5PM.

TheYale MFA in Photography is a celebrated two-year program of study admitting ten students a year. The program is committed to a broad definition of photography as a lens-based medium open to a variety of expressive means. Students work both individually and in groups with faculty and visiting artists.

Christian Badach’s photographs follow the life of a woman named Cedar, who suffers from hypermobility disorder. Through collaboration between artist and protagonist, the work uses their shared landscape of Western Massachusetts as a site to decode the ways seasonal cycles grant permissions and restrictions of movement, paradoxically affect emotions and change behavior. The camera functions as timekeeper, almanac and as anticipatory eulogy for a life suspended in limbo between daily pain and unflinching vigor, and for a contemporary landscape under threat. Through the merging of land and domesticity, Badach’s work grapples with themes of nontraditional caretaking, mortality, love and illness.

Chen Xiangyun employs photography, sculpture, video, installation, collaboration and archiving as strategies for queer world building. Rooted in their experience as a queer immigrant, Chen’s recent projects feature the billiards community in Flushing, New York, alongside psychologically probing portraits of diverse queer communities in the U.S. For this exhibition Chen will exhibit Jajang Billiards (2026), a 360-degree viewing of billiards culture in the Northeastern United States. A photographic assemblage of pool hall facades, cinematic movements through forgotten corners in the pool halls and stories from the legendary billiards players to amateurs, the work reveals the role billiards has played in the Asian and Latino communities. The project is in collaboration with Jinling Duan, sound designer, Ke Xu, projection designer and Jason Nuttle, Interactive Technologist.

Jasmine Clarke’s photographs capture small, fleeting moments of family life, engaging with the fragmented memories and embellished recollections that accumulate over time. By addressing a wide range of emotions present within familial histories—joy and difficulty, attachment and misunderstanding—Clarke reveals the everyday forces that shape both individual and collective identities. Through figures and cast shadows, Clarke’s compositions challenge perception within the context of domestic life.

Faith Couch’s practice centers self-depiction as a method of entering and reshaping visual histories that have excluded or flattened Black life. Through careful direction of wardrobe, lighting and composition, she constructs a visual language that exists between documentation and fabrication, grounded in truth yet heightened through emotional and symbolic resonance. Drawing on art historical and cinematic languages, Couch engages temporal reorientation and re-codes visual vocabularies through gesture, symbol and index. Centering the mundane as a site of resistance, her work produces haptic, multisensory images that affirm Black life as intimate, enduring and full of meaning.

Influenced by the idea of the photobooth—as a space where performance and self-presentation dovetail and where fictions, realities and a sense of place coexist—Christopher Postlewaite’s work consists of photographs made in collaboration with his spouse and extended network of friends. Augmenting the portraits, Postlewaite also photographs the landscape of Philadelphia and people’s lived environments: bars, nightclubs, homes and bedrooms.

In her self portraits, Olivia Reavey often contrasts her body in an assertive juxtaposition with industrial artifacts whereas in other works, she appears in scenes or performances born from moments of spontaneity. In these, friends or models, mostly male and often in the nude, participate in an awkward dance in which neither photographer nor subject knows the choreography. They sway and stomp across a dance floor of intimacy, intimidation and adoration—renegotiating the complex and murky histories of photographic representation and pre-established power dynamics.

John Shen’s multivalent and experimental practice approaches photography as both image and object, exploring the material, temporal and conceptual conditions through which photographs come to exist. Working across experimental photography, scientific optical systems and handmade imaging apparatuses, Shen frequently engages in early photographic technologies to reconsider his relationship between visibility, memory and representation.

For Em Wall photography and family are inexorably intertwined. Raised in a Mormon family in Michigan, they use photography to dismantle the domestic traditions and the family structure they were taught as a child. Now, their four children can be seen in Wall’s work representing themselves, the photographer and ideas of gender and sexuality in a religious family. Using the twin lens reflex their grandpa first gave to their mom, Wall’s photos use Chrisitan symbols to establish allegories where reality and fiction blend to provoke questions about religious and personal truth.

Andrew Warner’s work explores the abstraction of control and the phenomenon of perception surrounding attire. By using self-portraiture, performance, landscape and the portrait studio, he investigates the breakdown of one’s character as an act of endurance and the self as a site of interpretation.

Zach Ritter

“In Rooms is a complex meditation on the human psyche, sexuality, and the unconscious,” writes Richard McCabe, Curator of Photography at the Ogden Museum of Southern Art.

In Rooms began in the winter of 2011 as a visual diary, when visual artist Brittany Markert first picked up a 35mm camera and began using photography as a means of expression, escape, and the forming her inner worlds. What started as an intuitive method of survival has gradually evolved into an ongoing visual narrative, an abstract diary of the unconscious, primarily constructed through self-portraiture and staged interiors.

In her latest volume, In Rooms III, Markert continues her explorations into these psychologically charged dreamscapes. “This book is a testament of life, of choosing living,” she writes. “It is possible to live, to not fear death, to find stillness and clarity in every moment. The voices will pass, your thoughts do not define you. It is okay to be misunderstood.”

Rooted in analog photography and darkroom printing, In Rooms is shaped by slowness, ritual, and the uncertainty of photographic alchemy. The work draws from surrealism, occult symbolism, Jungian psychology, horror, cinema, and the emotional architecture of domestic spaces and relationship dynamics. Mirrors, veils, doorways, masks, and windows recur as symbolic thresholds between reality and the invisible. The body is a site of confrontation and transformation, moving over the years between seduction and sovereignty, collapse and resurrection, and silence and revelation.

“Brittany Markert’s compelling photographs are cinematic in scope, blending beauty and horror with the psychological elements of Surrealism and the dark, mysterious undertones of Southern Gothic literature and art. Her work follows a photographic trajectory that includes artists such as Ralph Eugene Meatyard and Clarence John Laughlin.”

“The truth is difficult to find through the distortion, but once you see her, nothing stays the same.” – Brittany Markert

Mémoire de l’Avenir (MDA) / Humanities, Arts and Society (HAS)brought together 10 transdisciplinary artists — from here and elsewhere for the exhibition Terrain de jeu !which has just closed.

This exhibition questions what games and sport reveal about our societies: power dynamics, competition, inclusion, everyday life, care of the body, and our capacity to live together.

Sport and games offer common ground not as solutions to social tensions, but as spaces in which to test methods, cross divides, and build understanding beyond differences.

Far from anecdotal, playful practices constitute systems governed by shared rules, where strategy, chance, cooperation, and fairness shape interactions.

Like the arts, play is a universal language that crosses cultures and territories, linking the urban and the rural, the individual and the collective, the intimate and the spectacular.

The artists examine contemporary social and political issues, or simply the care of the body and everyday life, through the prism of games and sport sometimes subverting or reinventing the rules, opening new spaces for encounter.

Original conceptAB SAMUEL– One, Two, Three Viva l’Algérie –-film- with Mémoire de l’Avenir

The World Cup crosses the globe, creating a paradoxical space one of both sharing and separation.

Its lines connect as much as they divide: neighborhoods, generations, cultures, and social classes.

Sport, far from neutral, reveals a grammar of power.

“The system loves symbolic victories. They’re cheaper than real change.” Naomi Klein

Erika Zollisent us her latest series Nóstos : The Return to Oneself, presented as follow.

In ancient Greek culture, nóstos was far more than the act of returning home. It described a transformative journey through which the hero ultimately rediscovered himself. Homer’s Odyssey remains its most enduring expression: after crossing unknown seas and enduring storms, enchantments, and countless trials, Odysseus’ return to Ithaca becomes inseparable from the recovery of his own identity.

In this series, water becomes a metaphor for that inner journey. Evoking the amniotic fluid from which life originates, it suggests a primordial return—not merely to a physical place, but to one’s truest self.

Immersed in this suspended dimension, the faces concealed by flowers relinquish their individual identity to evoke a universal human condition shaped by memory, vulnerability, and transformation. Deprived of recognizable features, they become mirrors in which viewers may recognize fragments of their own emotional experience.

Each work invites reflection on one’s personal nóstos: the path that, through time and lived experience, leads toward a deeper understanding of the self. In this sense, the artwork is not simply an image to be contemplated, but a presence that continues to engage in dialogue with those who choose to welcome it into their living space.

Erika Zolli

Image 73: Our Week Favorite: Marie Mons embarks on a kind of quest for identity in this photographic series, in which she once again explores the theme of the self-portrait. Throughout, she consistently questions appearances: those of her body, those of her own gaze, and those of our own… A reciprocal exchange of questions between the subject, the artist and the viewer, oscillating between certainties (what Marie knows about herself) and discoveries (what the final image might reveal by capturing what eludes us). Marie Mons, ‘Self-Portraits’, published in the journals of the Maison François Méchain @mariemons @lamaisonfrancoismechain Photo: © Marie Mons - Courtesy of the artist — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : Marie Mons poursuit une forme de quête d’identité dans cette série photographique où elle creuse à nouveau la question de l’autoportrait. Avec constance, elle y interroge les apparences : celles de son corps, celles de son propre regard, celles du nôtre… Réciprocité des questions entre le modèle, l’artiste et le spectateur, va et vient entre certitudes (ce que Marie sait d’elle-même) et découvertes (ce que l’image finale pourrait révèler en captant ce qui échappe). Image 75: Exhibition: Earlie Hudnall has been photographing Houston’s Third and Fourth Wards since the 1970s. Ces quartiers possèdent une histoire afro-américaine passionnante ; le Fourth Ward a été fondé par d’anciens esclaves affranchis. Earlie a saisi des images emblématiques des habitants de Houston et a connu une carrière longue et fructueuse, ses photographies figurant dans des collections de musées à travers tout le pays. A voir dans l'exposition 'From Sea To Shining Sea' à la PDNB Gallery.

Image 77: Biennale: In a landscape where major photography events are often concentrated in large cities, the Xavier Miserachs Photography Biennale champions a different vision of a festival: an event on a human scale that fosters a dialogue between local memory and contemporary issues. And among the Biennale’s many highlights is ‘Travailleurs de la mer’ by Carles Palacio, which focuses on the fishermen of the Costa Brava and the vulnerabilities of a profession under threat. @carlespalacio @biennalxmiserachs Photo: Serie Trabajadores del Mar, Costa Brava, 2018-2022 - Carles Palacio — — — — — Biennale : Dans un paysage où les grands rendez-vous de l’image restent souvent concentrés dans les grandes villes, la Biennale de photographie Xavier Miserachs défend une autre idée du festival ; une manifestation à taille humaine capable de faire dialoguer mémoire locale et enjeux actuels. Et parmi les nombreux points forts de la Biennale, « Travailleurs de la mer » de Carles Palacio, consacré aux pêcheurs de la Costa Brava et aux fragilités d’un métier menacé.

Image 79: Exhibition: 'My practice focuses on identity, emotional experience and the psychological spaces young people navigate, using image‑making to express what is often felt but not easily spoken. Je recourt à la création d'images pour exprimer ce qui est souvent ressenti mais difficilement formulé. Je travaille de manière expérimentale avec des procédés tels que la projection, le cyanotype, le tissu et les techniques photographiques en superposition, afin de créer des œuvres intimes et propices à la réflexion, ancrées dans l'expérience vécue. » — Sianna Campbell, au Travel Through Art Studio. #siennacampbell #traveltroughartstudio

Archives – August 6, 2020

As part of the Normandie impressionniste festival and the Cerisy conference devoted to color in photography, the MAP draws on its rich collections to trace the history of color photography, from its early technical difficulties to its current dominance. The exhibition takes place at the médiathèque in Saint-Lô, from August 1 to October 15, 2020.

Color photography was in its infancy at the end of the 19th century, and remained marginal until the Second World War. Hand-coloring techniques were the very first to answer the appeal of color: projection plates, prints, postcards. Autochrome plates, marketed from 1907, gave amateurs such as the young Lartigue the chance to immortalize their leisure pursuits. Professional use, however, remained limited to war photography, archaeology, architecture, and travel photography. In 1935 and 1936, flexible color film from Kodak and Agfa arrived, but this technical development spread little in France before the war.

After 1945, all the technical, industrial, social, and commercial elements came together to make greater use of color. Photographers such as André Kertész and Willy Ronis responded to commercial demand from the press and advertising, but black and white, for aesthetic and technical reasons, remained the preference of artists.

The status of color shifted in the 1970s and 1980s. Color photographs kept better, and it was during this period that photography became legitimized as an art form: markets, museums, and collectors entered the scene. Photographers gained a certain freedom and became less dependent on the press and commissions. Color processes then played a part in renewing or shaping the aesthetic of certain photographers, such as Daniel Boudinet, Dolorès Marat, and John Batho. Finally, digital technology in the 2000s once again upended these techniques, some of which disappeared, in favor of the artist’s total control over their photography, from the shot to the print.

Archives – August 6, 2021

The Fahey/Klein Gallery presents“Ernest Withers: I’ll Take You There”, an exhibition hosted in conjunction with his recently published book, “The Revolution in Black and White”(CityFiles Press). This exhibition and publication are a record of African American life in the South during the mid-20 th century. Withers’s photographs of Beale Street, family life in Memphis, the rise of Rock ‘n’ Roll and R&B, and the Civil Rights movement capture a time of radical change.

“Photography is a collection of memories. One who is trained in photography knows that. Instinctively, people who have an occupation know what they ought to do. You call the fireman to put out the fire; you call the police to solve a police problem; and people who are news people and journalists are collectors and recorders of present evidence, which after a given length of time—days, months, years becomes history.”Ernest C. Withers

Withers documented a history that still resonates today, capturing the momentous, and often dangerous, upheaval of America’s civil rights movement across the South from the late 1940’s through the 1960’s. Apart from documenting those fighting for racial justice and equity, Withers gained acclaim by capturing the African American experience, creating a singular record of day-to-day life in an effort to better illustrate and understand life in the South during this crucial era. His vast archive also includes images of famed Memphians who brought Soul, Rock ‘n’ Roll, and the Blues into the white, mainstream music scene. From blues to baseball, high school proms and football games to funerals and marches, and moments both mundane and historic, Withers was there, camera in hand. The confidence and skill he developed in the juke joints of Beale Street and on assignment for newspapers served him well when history happened. He was fearless in the face of intimidation, risking life and limb to get the shot.

Dr. Ernest C. Withers, Sr. (1922 – 2007) a native Memphian, is an internationally acclaimed photojournalist. His photographs have been published extensively in the New York Times, Washington Post, Time, Life, Jet, and Ebony. His well-known images comprise an unequaled time capsule of the heartland of Mid-Century America. Withers’s images are in the permanent collection of The Smithsonian and other esteemed institutions.

Revolution in Black and White: Photographs of the Civil Rights Era by Ernest C. Withers(CityFiles Press, 288 pages; $50) is available for purchase at the gallery while supplies last.
