This new book draws from the archives of photographer David Hurn to chronicle his career over a period of over 65-years. The making of this new book provided opportunity for Hurn to revisit and re-evaluate previously overlooked photographs with the benefits of time and experience, and to bring them to the fore. These lesser-seen photographs are published alongside some of his best-known works to demonstrate the longevity and breadth of his remarkable career.

The book opens with one of the first photographs ever taken by Hurn in 1955 in London, quickly followed by an image from the Hungarian Revolution in 1956—the reportage which helped to establish his reputation. Living in London during this period he became a visual narrator of the social revolution of the 1950s-1960s through changes in class and demographics whilst working for The Sunday Times, Queen Magazine and Town Magazine amongst others.

Hurn undertook numerous long-term projects in the US and the book includes a selection of this work ranging from street scenes in New York, to the deserts of California and Dolly Parton look-a-like competitions and group exercise classes in Arizona. Photographs taken across Europe in France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and Yugoslavia in the intervening years show his continued versatility, often documenting where tradition and customs collided with modernity.

Some of Hurn’s best-known photographs were taken in the aftermath of the Aberfan disaster in Wales in 1966. This event held a particular poignancy for the photographer and contributed to his decision to move back to Wales from London a few years later. Once there, his intention was to go beyond cliches to photograph Wales with all its complexities. Shortly after his return in 1973 he established the School of Documentary Photography in Newport at a time when the area was in the throes of deindustrialisation with high rates of unemployment,. His aim was to teach photography as a vocation to diversify the job market. After leaving the school in 1989, Hurn eventually turned away from documentary photojournalism to create work with a more personal approach, which he still creates today from his home in Tintern, Wales.

Born in Surrey, England in 1934, but of Welsh descent, David Hurn is a self-taught photographer who began his career in 1955 as an assistant at the Reflex Agency. He became an associate member of Magnum in 1965 and a full member in 1967. In 1973, he set up the School of Documentary Photography in Newport, Wales.

In 1997 he collaborated with Professor Bill Jay on the textbook, On Being a Photographer, which has been in print ever since. Hurn’s book Wales: Land of My Father, was the result of a self-initiated project attempting to discover what is meant by the phrase ‘my culture’. It observed changes taking place in Wales from 1970 until the book’s publication by Thames and Hudson in 2000. In 2016, Hurn was awarded an honorary fellowship of the Royal Photographic Society, and in 2020, the he was the recipient of a Lucie Award for Achievement in Documentary.

The Musée des Confluences in Lyon presents Corée du Nord ( North Korea) by Stéphan Gladieu.

Stéphan Gladieu is interested in closed societies, and in portraiture in particular, questioning the relationship between identity and appearance… Between 2017 and 2020, he traveled to North Korea five times where, despite strict supervision, he created a space of freedom within the constraints imposed on him.

His series, inspired by the visual codes of propaganda imagery, attempts to capture the individual within a society where only the collective matters and every single action is monitored. It decodes the regime’s daily staging.

It is a country we know little about… and with good reason: North Korea is one of the most closed dictatorships in the world.

Photographer Stéphan Gladieu traveled there five times to create a series of portraits between 2017 and 2020. Duly authorized to enter this country of absolute control, and accompanied at all times, he used his mobile photography studio to recreate a space of freedom, playing with backdrops and the visual codes of propaganda.

From the hair salon to the ice rink, from the factory to the rice paddy, some forty portraits open just as many windows onto everyday life in North Korea, documenting a pivotal moment in contemporary history.

Carefully composed, the frontal staging of the subjects offers a humanist approach to individuals usually absorbed into the collective. The treatment of color and the repetition of poses run through the exhibition as a guiding thread, between reality and representation, between individual identities and codified appearances. By sharing the story behind the photo sessions, Stéphan Gladieu also questions our relationship to images.

Before the camera, North Koreans look at us just as much as we observe them. But what do they see in us, and what do we really perceive of them?

Interview with Stéphan Gladieu

Why did you choose North Korea for this project?Over the years, working on major reportages, I realized I often ended up in places that were difficult to get into: dictatorships, closed places, secret societies… That’s why I’ve always been fascinated by North Korea. I tried for 15 years to get in, without success, until a chance meeting allowed me to meet North Korean representatives in France and obtain authorization to travel there.

What reality were you trying to show through your images?North Korea is a country where control is absolute, so my movements were subject to authorization, and I was supervised throughout my stay.

Imposing the portrait was a first challenge, but the photographic process I chose must have reassured them, since working in a static way certainly gave them the feeling of controlling the situation. Their relationship to perfection, to the polished side of things, the control they wish to have over life, as well as the overall aesthetic of their surroundings, push them to live in a society that is completely staged.

When you look at the photos, you sometimes get the impression that they’re fake, that they’re composites worked up on green screens, that there’s something stereotypical about them.

It’s actually deliberate, and what I photographed is real. The people you see are dressed like this when I encounter them, the backdrops exist… North Koreans live in that kind of society. That’s their way of life, that’s how they function.

What was your method for these portraits?I choose people in a completely random way. Experience has taught me that it was often linked to color combinations, but above all to people who move me, whatever their age or type. I always keep the same distance, 5 meters from the subject.

By marking a spot on the ground and asking people to stand there, I take care to always pair the person I’m photographing with a backdrop. It’s this encounter between the two that I love working with.

“A portrait is a mirror that teaches us as much about ourselves as about the person facing us.”

The Princeton University Art Museum presents Photography as a Way of Life: Minor White, Aaron Siskind, and Harry Callahan, an exhibition exploring the intertwined careers of three of the most influential photographers and teachers in mid-twentieth-century America. On view in Princeton through September 7, 2026, and then traveling, the exhibition draws on the rich photography holdings of the Princeton University Art Museum and its Minor White Archive to bring together iconic and previously unpublished color and black-and-white prints, rarely seen slides, and an array of published and archival materials that illuminate a vision of making a living and shaping a life through photography.

“Photography as a Way of Life highlights a pivotal historical moment when photography emerged as a serious academic discipline and a viable artistic profession, and thus as a way of being and living,” said James Steward, Nancy A. Nasher–David J. Haemisegger, Class of 1976, Director of the Princeton University Art Museum. “White, Siskind, and Callahan did more than make extraordinary photographs: They built institutions, communities, and ideas that continue to shape how photography is taught and valued today.”

Tracing the decades after World War II, Photography as a Way of Life explores how Minor White, Aaron Siskind, and Harry Callahan redefined photography as both an artistic practice and a professional vocation. Coming to the medium from distinct backgrounds and visual traditions, these three artists converged around shared commitments to abstraction, deeply personal expression, and the belief that photography could sustain a life’s work.

The exhibition takes its title from a recurring phrase in Minor White’s diaries and letters, in which he described photography as a “way of life.” For White, the phrase encompassed artistic ambition, pedagogy, and personal growth—a vision he advanced as a founding editor of Aperture, the influential photography magazine launched in 1952. Siskind and Callahan were central figures in White’s vision for the field, with their work prominently featured in Aperture alongside broader discussions of photographic education and postwar art photography.

“Princeton University holds a central place in the academic study of photography, with a proud legacy of stewardship and landmark scholarly exhibitions,” said Brendan Fay, exhibition curator. “The Minor White Archive is one of the cornerstones of that legacy, and it’s an honor to present an exhibition that builds on that strength during the new Museum’s inaugural year.”

From the 1940s through the 1970s, amid booming markets for Kodak snapshots and photojournalism, photography began to take root within higher education. White, Siskind, and Callahan were among the first generation of college-level photography teachers, developing models of photographic education during the GI Bill era that quickly spread across colleges and universities in the United States. While achieving critical success through books, exhibitions, and museum acquisitions, these artists also helped catalyze the creation of academic programs, publishing ventures, and professional societies that defined the postwar photographic landscape.

Highlights of the exhibition include a reconstruction of White’s Slow Dance, a projected sequence of color slides performed for live audiences in the late 1960s and 1970s, as well as materials from magazines and journals ranging from Popular Photography and Aperture to poetry publications and The Black Photographers Annual. The exhibition also traces the expansive networks shaped by these photographers, featuring works by more than forty additional artists, from Alfred Stieglitz and Dorothea Lange to Anthony Barboza and Donna-Lee Phillips.

The exhibition is accompanied by a richly illustrated exhibition catalogue copublished by the Museum and Princeton University Press.

Photography as a Way of Life is curated by Brendan Fay, associate professor of art history in the School of Art & Design at Eastern Michigan University and is organized and presented by the Princeton University Art Museum. Following its debut at Princeton, the exhibition will travel through 2028, with presentations at the High Museum of Art in Atlanta; the Addison Gallery of American Art in Andover, Massachusetts; and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City, Missouri.

Image 67: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 73: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. Archives – August 18, 2022

An American couple Robertand Shana ParkeHarrison’s fine art photography embodies a world of surreal and symbolic imagery, where Robert is the main character. Their photographs have been displayed in over 45 solo exhibitions and over 100 group shows worldwide and their work can also be found in over thirty-five collections, including the National Museum of American Art at the Smithsonian Institution, The George Eastman House, The Whitney Museum, LACMA, and SFMOMA. Their book, the Architect’s Brother was named as one of “the ten best photography books of the year in 2000 by the New York Times.”

“Our photographs offer visual poems of loss, human struggle and personal exploration with landscapes scarred by technology and over–use. As collaborative artists, we strive to link laborious actions, idiosyncratic rituals, and strangely crude machines metaphorically and poetically into tales about our contemporary experiences. We construct elaborate sets from found objects. Our scenes combine real and constructed landscapes. These scenes have a sense of determination and irony while addressing mankind’s responsibility to heal the damage inflicted on the environment.

Staged images offer endless possibilities for exploration while offering viewers personal interpretation. By allowing viewers to complete the story before them, we allow agency to take hold within them. We develop layers of duality, hope and despair, success and failure, desire and distain, destruction, and stewardship. We explore the fragile human condition, and overarching shadow of environmental destruction. Perhaps the only try hope for the world and our human spirit rests in our ability to imagine.” ParkHarrison

Links here to website: [https://www.parkeharrison.com](https://www.parkeharrison.com/)

Patricia Lanza: Your work focuses on the Anthropocene, the human effect on the earth. How did you come to use this as your theme and narrative?

ParkeHarrison: The Anthropocene, Global Warming, Climate Change, The End of Days, the Great Reckoning, The End of the World as we Know it. In the early 1990’s when our ideas began to gel into elusive yet cohesive imagery, these terms were not even discussed in media or popular culture. It was a concern for many scientists and academics but not the rest of us. We were in Graduate school in New Mexico. We were two naïve kids from suburban midwestern families. Beyond being sent to our rooms for failing to turn off the lights during the Energy Crisis, we had never even thought about Climate Change. Our exposure to the stunning raw beauty of the New Mexico landscape, the compelling religious practices and world view of the Hopi, along with other indigenous people, and as well as the overwhelming footprint of the US military, industrial complex (Los Alamos National Labs and White Sands/Trinity Site) These elements along with our tendencies toward performance-based photography and our desire to create art tied to purpose, merged into images focused on humankind’s behavior toward the Earth.

Patricia Lanza: Your work is a collaboration, how did this come about?

ParkeHarrison: Our collaboration grew organically over many years and many in depth conversations about art. We were each in grad school for creative endeavors. Our collaboration began as assisting one another, and slowly grew/ merging our interests and technical tendencies.

Patricia Lanza: As co-creators discuss your process in the development and construct of the photography including technically and content?

ParkeHarrison: Our process is layered with research, contemplation, and experimentation. Our images show a confluence of concerns and subjects that interest us including:

Politics, human behavior, theater, dance, religion, literature, film, environment topics, science, metaphysics and on and on. We typically begin new work by looking back at old work: how ideas worked as images, how they failed to fully embody our intent. We combine this information with topics of interest. From there we begin researching in a Butterfly effect sort of process. Ideas take us down rabbit holes where we find new interests. All of this searching leads to drawings. Drawings lead to the integration of props, often based on discarded materials and debunked devises. We then play with these objects, often inventing new purposes for

old machines. We begin testing images in the landscape and experimenting with possibilities beyond our initial ideas. Finally, we photograph images to be combined in either the darkroom or within photoshop. Once the images are printed they are not necessarily complete. Often they will be painted to enhance/encase them.

Patricia Lanza: You illustrate the theme in a surreal world full of symbolism. Where do you draw your inspiration?

ParkeHarrison: It would be great to walk in the store to the isle of inspiration! Making art takes daily practice, a honing of one’s skills and a constant inquisitive nature. We draw inspiration through constant focus.

Patricia Lanza: What or Who are your influences?

ParkeHarrison:Cultural and environmental writings, theater, film, dance, religion, politics, literature. Artists that come to mind today: Bill McKibben, Gabriel Garcia Márquez, Robert Wilson, Joseph Beuys, Andrei Tarkovsky, Wim Wenders, Louise Bourgeois, Pina Bausch, Ohad Naharin and so many more!

Patricia Lanza: How can and does the creation of ART have effect on important issues? What are you hoping for in yours?

ParkeHarrison: Visual art often involves the individual viewer forming his/her/their own interpretation of the artwork they are engaging. We attempt to create work that asks questions, work that allows the viewer to enter and form their own story, and personal meaning. We create work that is influenced by the philosophy of Joseph Beuys.

He believed art has the ability to promote change. By allowing viewers to engage freely within the world we create, viewers find their purpose and their response to the topics we speak to, most notably environment action.

Patricia Lanza: Discuss your latest photographic series and exhibition?

ParkeHarrison: We recently completed a small series of photo-lithographs titled, RED SUN. These images are fairly simple in their construction when compared to much of our work. Each print contains the isolated figure, the protagonist, engaging in actions, with Red interventions. While this was supposed to be a small suite of images we were inspired to continue this work involving interventions. Currently we are experimenting with ideas involving photographic imagery and sculptural components.

Alexandre de Metz –The Instinct for Image

A clear vision, a sharp eye, and a keen sense of the market. Alexandre de Metz embodies a new generation of cultural entrepreneurs who have successfully bridged the gap between artistic excellence and accessibility. As co-founder of YellowKorner—a brand that has become a global reference in the distribution of fine art photography, he has spent nearly two decades pursuing a singular ambition: to take photography out of closed circles and bring it into everyday life. But never at the cost of quality prints are entrusted to expert art labs, or to artistic integrity, with a curatorial line where legendary figures of contemporary photography meet promising new voices.

A graduate of ESSEC, trained in economics but driven by a deep love of culture, he launched YellowKorner in 2006 with his partner Paul-Antoine Briat. What began as a bold wager quickly grew into a phenomenon. Going against the grain of traditional galleries, they imagined a new way of collecting: more direct, more emotional, more free. Today, YellowKorner boasts over 130 galleries around the world—from Paris to Shanghai, New York to Dubai—promoting a cosmopolitan vision of photography at the crossroads of luxury, aesthetics, and visual storytelling.

Yet Alexandre de Metz is not defined by entrepreneurial success alone. He is a discerning enthusiast, as likely to cite Paolo Roversi as Sarah Moon, to be moved by a Robert Frank print or shaken by Juliette Hanrot’s Madonna of Bentalha. He speaks about photography as one might speak about music: with emotion, precision, and passion. What he seeks is what stirs, what halts, what displaces. Behind the entrepreneur lies an eye and behind the eye, a sensibility.

An insatiable collector, he hunts rare books, roams auction houses like one browses a secret library, and confesses a long-standing affection for darkened cinemas, piano recitals, and sad clowns captured by Nadar. At the intersection of commerce and the intimate, he represents a singular way of being with the images, aware of its power, but also its vulnerability.

A modern humanist, Alexandre de Metz believes photography has the power to shift perception, reveal invisible truths, and awaken consciousness. In a world saturated with visuals, he advocates for a more mindful gaze, more demanding, more embodied. A gaze that transcends time and speaks to the spirit of our age.

**www.yellowkorner.com

Instagram : @akthyrka / @yellowkorner_official**

Your first photographic spark?

It was the smell of chemical baths in Ousson-sur-Loire. I was around fifteen, making my first silver prints in the darkroom of our family home.

The image-maker who inspires you?

Clara Haskil. An exceptional pianist with a destiny of immense fragility and rare intensity. With her, it’s all about nuance and controlled tension.

The image you wish you had taken?

Probably one of the photographs from Richard Avedon’s American West series.

[![Image 32](blob:http://localhost/2d0d29bba129017e82cb1a2b1f706d29)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/01-avedon.jpg)

© The Richard Avedon Foundation

The one that moved you the most?

Recently, I rediscovered Jane Evelyn Atwood’s portrait of an incarcerated woman giving birth, lying on her bed a raw, frontal image of overwhelming intensity.

[![Image 34](blob:http://localhost/04f883e77b1fcfe07acc2412a8a2abe6)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2-jane-evelyn-atwood.jpg)

© Jane Evelyn Atwood

The one that made you angry?

Sebastião Salgado’s photographs of the Serra Pelada gold mines.

[![Image 36](blob:http://localhost/6581f739dfefeb9cb4af6cdecb463fcf)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/03-salgado.jpg)

© Sebastião Salgado

A photographic memory from your childhood?

A stolen photograph taken with my first film camera: a farmer and his cows in the morning fog of the Loire Valley.

The image that haunts you?

One of Paolo Roversi’s portraits of Natalia.

[![Image 38](blob:http://localhost/96bff639790bbc94e3d93de0f379f7a2)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/04-roversi.jpg)

© Paolo Roversi

The one that changed the world?

Dali Atomicus by Philippe Halsman—a technical and creative tour de force.

[![Image 40](blob:http://localhost/3b5dcdaa268e756de8e429ae82c7645e)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/05-halsman.jpg)

© Philippe Halsman

The one that changed your world?

My parents’ wedding photo, in black and white, with a row of altar boys an image suspended in time.

If budget were no limit, which artwork would you dream of acquiring?

An original print from Robert Frank’s The Americans. This book is a visual and narrative punch. It speaks of the fragility, loneliness, and beauty in the margins of a country and an era.

[![Image 42](blob:http://localhost/ac6813d1c9c493a6021f6920a6c80bff)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/frank-bus-small.jpg)

© Robert Frank

In your opinion, what quality does a good photographer need?

Photography is writing with light you must have the image in your mind before you even press the shutter, yet still be open to reality surpassing and surprising you.

The secret to the perfect image, if it exists?

It doesn’t exist. But if it stops you, if it speaks in silence, then it is right. Avedon said, “All photographs are accurate. None of them is the truth.”

The person you’d like to photograph?

A jazz band in full swing or seemingly ordinary families, as Tina Barney did.

[![Image 44](blob:http://localhost/1edc82f484efecd79b209b6cccc93f3f)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/06-tina-barney.jpg)

© Tina Barney

The person you’d like to be photographed by?

Jamie Hawkesworth, for his ability to suspend time and bring grace out of silence or Elizaveta Porodina for her boundless creativity.

[![Image 46](blob:http://localhost/3ee0ae8b19d8432b222473ac3597b652)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/07-jamie-hawkesworth.jpg)

© Jamie Hawkesworth

[![Image 48](blob:http://localhost/3a6e9624dc119b148777fdf15d0b7b6f)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/07a-elizaveta-porodina.jpg)

© Elizaveta Porodina

A must-have photo book?

Blue Note: Photographs of Francis Wolff. A whole era, a style, a way of listening with your eyes.

Your childhood camera?

A Rolleiflex 6×6 2.8 Planar. I was fascinated by it you had to look into a well of light and frame at waist level: a discreet and direct gaze.

The one you use today?

An iPhone, like everyone else. But I keep my cameras like talismans.

Your favorite addiction?

Auction houses until midnight. I hunt for rare books, invisible editions, like treasure.

Your best way to disconnect?

A piano concert. The dark room and the silence before the first note already carry you away.

What’s your relationship with the image?

The image is immediate. Photography is memory. An image tells. A photograph touches. They are two different visual regimes. Often, the image reassures, and the photograph destabilizes.

Your greatest quality?

Curiosity. I’m always looking for a new perspective.

Your last extravagance?

An original drawing by Akira Toriyama, who passed away last year.

An image to illustrate a new banknote?

Sarah Bernhardt by dressed as a clown for its cynicism.

[![Image 50](blob:http://localhost/683ae2b3956be069ee0c3494da6a2d25)](https://loeildelaphotographie.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/08-nadar.jpg)

© Nadar

A job you would never want to do?

Politician.

Your greatest professional extravagance?

Co-founding YellowKorner in 2006. No one expected us. We went all in. It was dizzying, intense, sometimes insane, but always sincere and passionate.

Does photography have the power to change collective perception of an event or era?

Absolutely. I think of Juliette Hanrot’s photo La Madone de Bentalha, of a woman silently screaming in 1997 near Algiers. She holds her murdered child in her arms. The image transcends testimony to become an icon of civil suffering and the horror of war. It etched itself into minds, crystallizing both a mother’s unspeakable pain and the absurdity of violence. Through that photo, the view of the Algerian conflict shifted it became a universal human tragedy.

How do you view the influence of social media on the way photographs are made and perceived today?

Instagram is a multiplied mirror sometimes flattering, often distorting. But it also gives photography greater visibility and accessibility. It’s up to us to embrace innovation while preserving photographic standards.

An Instagram account not to miss?

I follow more and more curated accounts that offer inspiring feeds and let you discover authors—sometimes emerging ones. One example is The Analog Club, where every post opens a door into a photographic world. (@the.analog.club)

What’s the last thing you did for the first time?

Re-read a book for the third time: Journey to the End of the Night by Céline.

What makes a successful photo?

It’s a photo that stops you for a fraction of a second or for a lifetime.

What’s the difference between photography and fine art photography?

Photography records; fine art photography interprets. One documents; the other transforms.

The city, country, or culture you dream of discovering?

North Korea, which moved me deeply on an artistic and photographic level. I’m thinking in particular of Philippe Chancel’s work. I would love to see it with my own eyes.

A place you never tire of?

Vézelay a village steeped in mystery where spirituality is ever-present. Everything becomes reflection and silence.

Your greatest regret?

Not saying yes when I was asked to photograph James Brown. I didn’t believe it at the time.

Color or black and white?

I have deep respect for silver black and white, but when mastered, color becomes a form of writing.

Daylight or artificial light?

Natural light.

In your opinion, the most photogenic city?

It’s hard to choose, but I’d say New York.

If I could host your ideal dinner, who would be at the table?

My wife if Vivian Maier would kindly babysit. Fun fact: she was a nanny.

If God existed, would you ask Him to pose or take a selfie?

I think I’d ask Him to sign a contract so I could distribute the photo through YellowKorner.

An image that represents the current state of the world?

A photo by Alex Webb: layers of life, gazes that ignore each other, a saturation of images, or a photo by Martin Parr.

If you had to start over?

I wouldn’t start over I’d keep going. I believe in building step by step. This is only the beginning.

Note from the Publishing DirectorCarole Schmitz has complete editorial freedom over her Questionnaires.

Their tone can sometimes reflects, as is the case here, a different editorial line from that of L’Oeil de la Photographie.

In fact, L’Oeil de la Photographie does not support YellowKorner’s commercial approach.

Jean-Jacques Naudet / Publishing Director

Last Tuesday, we published the first part of our conversation with Jeremy Dennis, a contemporary photographer and enrolled member of the Shinnecock Indian Nation whose work explores Indigenous identity, history, and the relationship between people and place.

In that first installment, Dennis introduced the project that has become the foundation of his artistic practice, On This Site, an ongoing effort to map and document Indigenous history across Long Island. He spoke about the years of research behind the project, his commitment to making historical knowledge more accessible, and how this work naturally expanded into several interconnected photographic series, including Nothing Happened Here, Sacredness of Hills, and The Lazy. Together, these projects examine the relationship between land, memory, visibility, and contemporary Indigenous presence. In this second part, we focus more closely on Nothing Happened Here, discussing how Dennis uses staged photography, symbolism, and portraiture to invite viewers to reflect on history, shared responsibility, and the importance of empathy.

The title Nothing Happened Here directly contradicts the violent scenes we see. What kind of denial, whether political, educational, or social, are you critiquing with this phrase, and what conversations do you hope non-Native or international viewers will start after encountering this work?

One of the big things, not only behind this series, but around all my different projects, is the hope of creating connection and empathy. The project mostly features Caucasian subjects with these arrows impaled in them, but it’s supposed to talk about our connection, the history that we both share as Americans, Native or non-Native Americans. I do want people to walk away thinking about their connection to that story. And growing up here in Suffolk County in Southampton, in the Hamptons, it’s such a separated place, economically, racially, geographically, even public and private schools, jobs are separate, beach access separates people. So, I think a lot about why there are all these barriers when it’s so easy for us to get together.

The other side that inspires my work is similar to this article from Teen Vogue called Invisibility is the Modern Form of Racism Against Native Americans, and it talks about statistics about Native visibility. I always paraphrase the article, but there’s like a staggering number of people who don’t know a single Native American. And a lot of my work is myself coming out of my shell, being a shy person, approaching people, and asking them not only if I can take your photo, but also if I can set you up in this crazy scene. Can you represent this story, standing in for many other people? And it is just a lot of creating new friendships or connections, and it is special because sometimes these end up in shows, exhibits, or collections you never even imagined.

I believe I started this project at the Vermont Studio Center in 2018. And I was so hesitant myself because I’m not a very violent or confrontational person, and I was getting ready to quit. One of the artists who came to the studio visit is Steve Locke. He’s an African American visual artist, I think, in New York City. He’s a teacher as well. But he confirmed the value of the project and how important it is to tell that story. Since then, I’ve just had that same mindset that any image that comes to mind, you just have to do it, even if it’s a good or bad idea, just to get out there and out of your head. Lately, I’ve been going through the archive of digital negatives and seeing all the good work I skipped over because of that old way of thinking. The Nothing Happened Here series is just all about that connection and showing people that there is something between people or cultures, and even if you’re non-American, I think just being here, even as a visitor, there are a lot of ways that you can connect with Native people.

In that same series, Nothing Happened Here, you mentioned the emotional contrast between their calmly standing and posing and their being visibly pierced with arrows. Can you tell us how you want viewers to interpret this? How does it inform in terms of Indigenous histories of violence and survival?

I’m sure we’re going to get to it more later in the conversation, but we were talking about humor as well earlier. And the work is very serious and somber. But at the same time, I’m always looking at pop culture for inspiration. That’s why the work, in my opinion, stays in people’s minds so much, because it takes something familiar that maybe people see too often or maybe something they like and see it in a new light. I think looking back on this project, it reminds me of all those depression commercials, like there’s some ghosts or some wave or some goo that’s following you and ruining everything. And I wanted to relate that to this project because we have that new saying, Make America Great. There are so many reasons why you can’t make it great. It wasn’t great in the past, but I think one reason is the need for reconciliation with tribal communities. So it is supposed to be interpreted as something that we carry, but it’s like a delayed effect, and it’s also supposed to be moments of idleness. I think there’s a lot of that in writing and art, like the things that we think about when we’re finally done with the 9-to-5, and we’re trying to get motivated, but then childhood memory or trauma comes forth. So, that realization runs through a lot of the images as well.

This concludes the second part of our conversation with Jeremy Dennis. In the final interview, we will discuss his ongoing series Rise, his use of staged and digitally constructed photography, and the role of image-making in challenging inherited narratives while opening new ways of seeing Indigenous presence today.

Marie Audier D’Alessandris

The DGPh honours two defining figures of the international photographic art market – award ceremony to take place during Paris Photo Week in November

The German Photographic Society (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Photographie – DGPh) is presenting the inaugural Gruber Award to New York-based gallerist, photography expert and collector Howard Greenberg and Belgian collector, philanthropist and founder of A Foundation Astrid Ullens de Schooten Whettnall. An independent international jury selected them as the first recipients of the new distinction.

The Gruber Award was initiated by Thomas Gerwers, Chairman of the DGPh Art, Market & Law Section. Developed to mark the Section’s 25th anniversary, it is the first award in the DGPh’s 75-year history to focus specifically on the photographic art market and the individuals who shape it.

The award recognises gallerists, collectors, patrons and other mediators who create visibility for photography, foster artistic careers, preserve works and connect artistic production with the market, institutions and the wider public. It commemorates Renate and L. Fritz Gruber, who together assembled one of the most important photographic collections of their time. L. Fritz Gruber was among the founders of the DGPh in 1951 and, as a collector, cultural mediator and co-initiator of photokina, embodied the relationship between photography, the market and the public sphere.

August 19 holds a special place in the history of our medium. On this date in 1839, the French government officially announced the invention of the daguerreotype, a breakthrough created by Louis Daguerre, declaring it a free gift to the world. Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre was a French artist, photographer, and inventor best known for creating the daguerreotype, the first widely adopted photographic process. In 1839, France released the daguerreotype “free to the world,” revolutionizing art, science, and portraiture. His legacy remains foundational in photography’s history.That landmark moment gave birth to World Photography Day, an annual global celebration of visual storytelling, light, and creative expression.

To honor this legacy, photographer and founder of Suspect Photography Education, David Brommer, is leading a guided photowalk through the historic winding streets of Cortona, Italy, and acclaimed author of Agreeable Strangers, Charles Chessler will be leading a similar photo walk in NYC’s Central Park.

Brommer’s Cortona, Italy Celebration Photo Walk

Our journey begins in the open surroundings of Piazza Garibaldi, offering panoramic views over the Valdichiana. From there, David will guide the group on a steady uphill walk through Cortona’s timeless stone alleyways, capturing the morning light, historic architecture, and subtle moments of Tuscan life along the way.

The walk culminates at the highest point in town, the historic Fortezza del Girifalco. Upon arrival, we will explore the featured exhibitions of Cortona On The Move, the world renowned festival dedicated to contemporary visual narrative. After touring the exhibitions, we will gather for lunch together at the bistro located inside the Fortezza grounds.

Whether you carry a mirrorless camera, a film camera, or a smartphone, this walk offers a chance to refine your visual eye, discuss composition with fellow enthusiasts, and mark World Photography Day in an extraordinary setting.

Event Details

Date: Wednesday, August 19, 2026

Meeting Time: 9:00 AM CEST

Starting Location: Piazza Garibaldi, Cortona

Destination: Fortezza del Girifalco

RSVP: No RSVP necessary, simply show up and meet at the piazza.

Admission: Entry ticket to the Fortezza is not included; participants purchase tickets at the gate.

Follow Up: Information regarding an online review session held a few days later will be provided directly at the meet up.

'A Closer Look' de Bruce Gilden est publié aux éditions Skira. #Skira #Photobook #BruceGilden

Image 65: Rencontres d'Arles 2026: Alam’s exhibition, Ozymandias (2020–ongoing), is an intimate and multidisciplinary body of work that examines memory, identity, and cognitive decline through the artist’s experience of caring for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. @alampanah @rencontresarles Photo: Ozymandias © Aman Alam — — — — — Rencontres d'Arles 2026 : L'exposition d'Alam, « Ozymandias » (2020–en cours), est un ensemble d'œuvres intimistes et multidisciplinaires qui explore la mémoire, l'identité et le déclin cognitif à travers l'expérience vécue par l'artiste lorsqu'il s'est occupé de sa grand-mère après qu'elle eut reçu un diagnostic de maladie d'Alzheimer. S'appuyant sur la photographie, la sculpture, l'intelligence artificielle et des archives familiales, ce projet explore ce que signifie se souvenir, oublier et prendre soin d'une personne dont le sentiment d'identité s'effrite progressivement. #arles #amanaman

Image 67: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 69: Book: Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Jo Ann Chaus, 'Unspoken' is published by Kehrer Verlag. @joann_chaus @kehrerverlag Photo: © Jo Ann Chaus / Kehrer Verlag — — — — — Livre : Jo Ann Chaus incarne une série de stéréotypes et d’archétypes féminins des figures façonnées par des attentes héritées et des rôles intériorisés. Bien qu’elle soit une femme moderne et indépendante, l’artiste a dû reconnaître à quel point elle demeurait encore attachée à la génération de sa mère, guidée par les idéaux de l’épouse dévouée et de la mère sacrifiée. 'Unspoken' est un livre publié aux éditions Kehrer Verlag. #joannchaud #kehrerverlag

Image 73: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 75: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 77: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 79: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

Image 81: Portfolio: ‘Pacific Insomnia’ is an ongoing photographic series shot in French Polynesia. Every year, travelling funfairs stop off in Tahiti for a few weeks before moving on. For many of the island’s inhabitants, they offer a rare form of entertainment and form an integral part of a seasonal ritual. Like Hélène Havard, send us your portfolios. @helenehavard_travel Photo: © Hélène Havard Portfolio : « Pacific Insomnia » est une série photographique en cours réalisée en Polynésie française. Chaque année, des fêtes foraines itinérantes font escale à Tahiti pendant quelques semaines avant de repartir. Pour de nombreux habitants de l’île, elles constituent un divertissement rare et font partie intégrante d’un rituel saisonnier. Comme Hélène Havard, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #helenehavard

Image 83: Exhibition: Jerry Schatzberg belongs to a rare group of photographers who understood that performance does not begin on stage or end when the curtain falls. In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. On view at Holden Luntz Gallery. @schatzbergarchive @onlyediesedgwick @holdenluntzgallery Photo: Jerry Schatzberg, Edie Sedgwick, Slash, New York 1966, Silver Gelatin Photograph © Jerry Schatzberg - Courtesy Holden Luntz Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Jerry Schatzberg appartient à ce groupe restreint de photographes qui ont compris que la performance ne commence pas sur scène et ne s’achève pas à la tombée du rideau. Dans ses photographies, les mondes de la musique, de la mode, de la danse et de la célébrité ne se réduisent jamais à la publicité ou à la pose. Ils se révèlent au contraire à travers le geste, le rythme, l’atmosphère et la présence. #jerryschatzberg #ediesedgwick #holdenluntz

Image 85: Portfolio: On view for eleven days on the walls of the Ramallah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026, Mélissa Waucquier’s Fair Mur is a public photographic installation comprising portraits, rehearsal scenes and candid moments. @melissa_waucquier Photo: Melissa Waucquier, from the series 'Faire Mur', 2026, Ramal lah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026 © Melissa Waucquier — — — — — Portfolio: Deployée pendant onze jours sur les murs du Ramallah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026, Fair Mur de Mélissa Waucquier est une installation photographique ouverte au public, composée de portraits, de scènes de répétition et d’instantanés. #ramallah #melissawaucquier

Image 87: Exhibition: Yancey Richardson announces 'Once More, With Feelin'g, a group exhibition highlighting the work of the 2026 Yale MFA graduates in photography: Christian Badach, Chen Xiangyun, Jasmine Clarke, Faith Couch, Christopher Postlewaite, Olivia Reavey, John Shen, Em Wall and Andrew Warner. @jcklbyfsh @yalephoto @yanceyrichardsongallery Photo: Congregation, 2026 © John Shen - Courtesy Yancey Richardson — — — — — Exposition : Yancey Richardson annonce 'Once More, With Feeling', une exposition collective mettant en lumière le travail des diplômés 2026 du MFA de photographie de Yale : Christian Badach, Chen Xiangyun, Jasmine Clarke, Faith Couch, Christopher Postlewaite, Olivia Reavey, John Shen, Em Wall et Andrew Warner. #yale #yanceyrichardson

The Graham Foundation is honored to announce 45 new grants to organizations. Selected from more than 275 submissions, the funded projects include exhibitions, installations, publications, podcasts, films, student-led journals, international architecture events, and other public programs. The grantees range from major cultural institutions and independent nonprofit spaces to academic institutions, publishers, and community-based initiatives. Collectively, the projects advance new interdisciplinary ideas on architecture and design and engage publics around the world.

The new grants highlight work by established and emerging architects, artists, curators, designers, historians, scholars, writers, and others working with organizations worldwide in cities such as Boston, Buenos Aires, Frankfurt, London, Los Angeles, Mexico City, Montreal, Nairobi, New York, Pittsburgh, Seattle, St. Louis, Vienna, Zurich, and Chicago, where the Graham Foundation is based.

The Photography+ Emerging Talent returns for its second edition. With more than 1300 submissions from across the world, this initiative still builds on the simple idea that started it: talent does not only come with a qualification.

We welcomed submissions from anyone within the first five years of their practice, with or without a degree or postgraduate qualification. The result is a celebration of emerging voices from around the world, bringing together a diverse range of perspectives and approaches to photography.

This issue features the work of Lèa Chen (TW/UK), Tamás Cseke (HU), Angus Fayers (UK), Joel Jimenez Jara (CR), Grace Tenneh Kromah (US), Grace Martella (IT), Alice Poyzer (UK), Paula Elena Ramos (ES), Diana Sosnowska (IT/PL/US), Farhad Yasavoli (IR/UK). This year’s jury was composed by Emma Bowkett, Director of Photography at the Financial Times; Louise Fedotov-Clements, Director at Photoworks; Fernanda Prado Verčič, Founding Director of Kranj Foto Fest; Maryam Wahid, Head of Programs and Outreach at Tasweer Photo Festival; and Amin Yousefi, Assistant Curator and Editor of Photography+.

The issue also features a written feature by Nienke Coers, one of our 2026 writers in residence, exploring the work of this year’s winners.

Image 57: The Questionnaire: With Afghanistan, his most personal project to date, Daniel Malikyar undertakes a form of visual reclamation. He photographs a country that is not only the land of his origins, but also the bearer of a collective memory he inherited without ever having fully experienced it. There is, ultimately, something in this approach that extends beyond the Afghan questions alone. What does it mean to photograph a country when it already exists in the world’s imagination before the shutter is even released? When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 73: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. We are still in the midst of the major event devoted to Giono and Photography. It is in this context that his granddaughter, Agnès Durbet Giono, (a visual artist) and our colleague Henri Kartmann, are showing two very different series of works, with one thing in common: Jean Giono.

To begin with, it is worth knowing that Jean Giono was a great lover of photography other people’s, that is. He himself owned no camera and never took pictures. Instead, he would rummage everywhere in search of a photograph, a family album, a photographic collection. Then, discovering and leafing through his finds, he would extract certain portraits to turn into characters for his literary wanderings. He loved photographs and made them a vehicle for his thoughts.

It is from this habit that Agnès Durbet Giono, drawing on the personal memories she has kept of it, has set out to reinterpret the use of these images. Her approach relies on her more graphic, visual-artist’s touch to bring a new setting to images of the past. The use of gouache, watercolor, and unconventional supports serves the continuity of this heritage.

The approach is interesting and highly appealing. That said, the volumetric presence of the photographs within the piece remains somewhat under-proportioned. The photograph ought to be the starting point for reading each image, anchoring the shift into the artist’s fascinating universe. Having to solve a kind of initial riddle to find the start of the thread can discourage the uninitiated. That is a shame, because the approach, running parallel to Jean Giono’s own, is truly rooted in a passion examined from every angle.

It is regrettable, for the artist, that the limited resources granted by local authorities for showcasing this work force lay visitors to make an extra effort to interpret it properly.

I urge you to go not to see, but to immerse yourself in this exhibition. Agnès’s passions generate the atmosphere; her atmosphere satisfies the passion.

In the second part of the exhibition, Henri Kartmann presents photographs of the Durance, made after the texts of Jean Giono. I presented the works from this exhibition in this same magazine on September 5, 2023. I refer you to that article.

Thierry Maindrault

In Niort (France), la Villa Pérochon presents the exhibition L’image et la page : Carte blanche aux éditions lamaindonne(The Image and the Page: Carte Blanche for Lamaindonne Publishing).

.

“The photobook has a singularity that sets it apart from other art books. Unlike works devoted to painting, sculpture, or installation which show reproductions of works that exist elsewhere it is constituted of the work itself. Photography is, in fact, a reproducible medium: the image printed in the book is not a mere representation of a work, but one of its forms of existence. The book is therefore not a mediator between the reader and the work. It allows for direct experience of the work, with no intermediary.” David Fourré, head of éditions lamaindonne

This summer, the Villa Pérochon explores this strong bond between photography and publishing by inviting éditions lamaindonne. Built around 8 photographers, this group exhibition reveals the work carried out jointly by photographers and their editor.

SKIRA publishes Vision by Justine Tjallinks, a new monograph on a virtuoso photographer.

Vision is much more than a photography book: it is a sensory experience, an invitation to relearn how to see. In this book, Justine Tjallinks presents a body of work in which each image is born from an inner gesture, carefully considered long before any encounter with the model.

Photography becomes a space for rigorous composition, nourished by pictorial inspiration inherited from the Flemish masters, where light, posture and texture interact with silent precision. On the border between reality and imagination, her portraits are constructed layer by layer, revealing a restrained, profound, almost meditative presence.

Behind this masterful aesthetic lies a deeply human and committed approach. The artist asserts a feminine gaze freed from the rigid norms of beauty and visual hierarchies inherited from history. She celebrates long-marginalised singularities: non-standard bodies, faces bearing complex stories, visible or invisible differences. Without exoticism or voyeurism, Justine Tjallinks seeks the truth of the gaze and the expressive power of what disturbs and moves us. Vision offers another way of perceiving the world, where difference becomes an essential value and beauty is revealed in fragility, vulnerability and encounter.

A powerful and necessary book that transforms the act of looking into an act of consciousness.

Co-published with Sophie Scheidecker Gallery.

Image 69: Rencontres d'Arles 2026: Alam’s exhibition, Ozymandias (2020–ongoing), is an intimate and multidisciplinary body of work that examines memory, identity, and cognitive decline through the artist’s experience of caring for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. @alampanah @rencontresarles Photo: Ozymandias © Aman Alam — — — — — Rencontres d'Arles 2026 : L'exposition d'Alam, « Ozymandias » (2020–en cours), est un ensemble d'œuvres intimistes et multidisciplinaires qui explore la mémoire, l'identité et le déclin cognitif à travers l'expérience vécue par l'artiste lorsqu'il s'est occupé de sa grand-mère après qu'elle eut reçu un diagnostic de maladie d'Alzheimer. Image 71: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 73: Book: Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Jo Ann Chaus, 'Unspoken' is published by Kehrer Verlag. @joann_chaus @kehrerverlag Photo: © Jo Ann Chaus / Kehrer Verlag — — — — — Livre : Jo Ann Chaus incarne une série de stéréotypes et d’archétypes féminins des figures façonnées par des attentes héritées et des rôles intériorisés. Bien qu’elle soit une femme moderne et indépendante, l’artiste a dû reconnaître à quel point elle demeurait encore attachée à la génération de sa mère, guidée par les idéaux de l’épouse dévouée et de la mère sacrifiée. 'Unspoken' est un livre publié aux éditions Kehrer Verlag. #joannchaud #kehrerverlag

Image 77: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 79: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 81: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 83: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

Image 85: Portfolio: ‘Pacific Insomnia’ is an ongoing photographic series shot in French Polynesia. Every year, travelling funfairs stop off in Tahiti for a few weeks before moving on. For many of the island’s inhabitants, they offer a rare form of entertainment and form an integral part of a seasonal ritual. Like Hélène Havard, send us your portfolios. @helenehavard_travel Photo: © Hélène Havard Portfolio : « Pacific Insomnia » est une série photographique en cours réalisée en Polynésie française. Chaque année, des fêtes foraines itinérantes font escale à Tahiti pendant quelques semaines avant de repartir. Pour de nombreux habitants de l’île, elles constituent un divertissement rare et font partie intégrante d’un rituel saisonnier. Comme Hélène Havard, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #helenehavard

Image 87: Exhibition: Jerry Schatzberg belongs to a rare group of photographers who understood that performance does not begin on stage or end when the curtain falls. In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. On view at Holden Luntz Gallery. @schatzbergarchive @onlyediesedgwick @holdenluntzgallery Photo: Jerry Schatzberg, Edie Sedgwick, Slash, New York 1966, Silver Gelatin Photograph © Jerry Schatzberg - Courtesy Holden Luntz Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Jerry Schatzberg appartient à ce groupe restreint de photographes qui ont compris que la performance ne commence pas sur scène et ne s’achève pas à la tombée du rideau. Dans ses photographies, les mondes de la musique, de la mode, de la danse et de la célébrité ne se réduisent jamais à la publicité ou à la pose. Ils se révèlent au contraire à travers le geste, le rythme, l’atmosphère et la présence. #jerryschatzberg #ediesedgwick #holdenluntz

After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

For many of the island’s inhabitants, they offer a rare form of entertainment and form an integral part of a seasonal ritual. Like Hélène Havard, send us your portfolios. @helenehavard_travel Photo: © Hélène Havard Portfolio : « Pacific Insomnia » est une série photographique en cours réalisée en Polynésie française. Chaque année, des fêtes foraines itinérantes font escale à Tahiti pendant quelques semaines avant de repartir. Pour de nombreux habitants de l’île, elles constituent un divertissement rare et font partie intégrante d’un rituel saisonnier. Comme Hélène Havard, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #helenehavard

In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. On view at Holden Luntz Gallery. @schatzbergarchive @onlyediesedgwick @holdenluntzgallery Photo: Jerry Schatzberg, Edie Sedgwick, Slash, New York 1966, Silver Gelatin Photograph © Jerry Schatzberg - Courtesy Holden Luntz Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Jerry Schatzberg appartient à ce groupe restreint de photographes qui ont compris que la performance ne commence pas sur scène et ne s’achève pas à la tombée du rideau. Dans ses photographies, les mondes de la musique, de la mode, de la danse et de la célébrité ne se réduisent jamais à la publicité ou à la pose. Ils se révèlent au contraire à travers le geste, le rythme, l’atmosphère et la présence. #jerryschatzberg #ediesedgwick #holdenluntz
