Image 57: Exhibition: North Korea is one of the most closed dictatorships in the world. Stéphan Gladieu traveled there five times to create a series of portraits between 2017 and 2020. Duly authorized to enter this country of absolute control, and accompanied at all times, he used his mobile photography studio to recreate a space of freedom, playing with backdrops and the visual codes of propaganda. @stephangladieu @musee_des_confluences Photo: North Koreans Portraits North Korea PyongYang June 2018 Kim Yun Gyong, Han Sol Gyong, Kim Won Gyong, Kang Sun Hwa and Kong Su Hyang in the 3D movie theater at SCI Tech Complex. © Stéphan Gladieu - Courtesy Musée des Confluences — — — — — Exposition : La Corée du Nord est l’une des dictatures les plus fermées au monde. Stéphan Gladieu s’y est rendu à cinq reprises pour réaliser une série de portraits entre 2017 et 2020. Ayant obtenu l’autorisation nécessaire pour entrer dans ce pays soumis à un contrôle absolu, et accompagné en permanence, il a utilisé son studio de photographie mobile pour recréer un espace de liberté, en jouant avec les arrière-plans et les codes visuels de la propagande. #stephanegladieu #museedesconfluences #northkorea

Image 59: Exhibition: The Photography+ Emerging Talent returns for its second edition. With more than 1300 submissions from across the world, this initiative still builds on the simple idea that started it: talent does not only come with a qualification. This issue features the work of Lèa Chen (TW/UK), Tamás Cseke (HU), Angus Fayers (UK), Joel Jimenez Jara (CR), Grace Tenneh Kromah (US), Grace Martella (IT), Alice Poyzer (UK), Paula Elena Ramos (ES), Diana Sosnowska (IT/PL/US), Farhad Yasavoli (IR/UK). @takenbyleachen @photoworks_uk Photo: Longing for the Spring Breeze 2026 © Léa Chen — — — — Exposition : Le concours « Photography+ Emerging Talent » revient pour sa deuxième édition. Avec plus de 1 300 candidatures venues du monde entier, cette initiative reste fidèle à l’idée simple qui est à l’origine de sa création : le talent ne se résume pas à un diplôme. Ce numéro présente les travaux de Lèa Chen (Taïwan/Royaume-Uni), Tamás Cseke (Hongrie), Angus Fayers (Royaume-Uni), Joel Jimenez Jara (CR), Grace Tenneh Kromah (US), Grace Martella (IT), Alice Poyzer (UK), Paula Elena Ramos (ES), Diana Sosnowska (IT/PL/US) et Farhad Yasavoli (IR/UK).

Image 61: The Questionnaire: With Afghanistan, his most personal project to date, Daniel Malikyar undertakes a form of visual reclamation. He photographs a country that is not only the land of his origins, but also the bearer of a collective memory he inherited without ever having fully experienced it. There is, ultimately, something in this approach that extends beyond the Afghan questions alone. What does it mean to photograph a country when it already exists in the world’s imagination before the shutter is even released? Afghanistan, a 240-page book published by teNeues / Die Gestalten Verlag. @dmalikyar ✍️ A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: © Daniel Malikyar - Courtesy teNeues — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Avec Afghanistan, son projet le plus personnel, Daniel Malikyar entreprend alors une forme de reconquête visuelle. Il photographie un pays qui n’est pas seulement celui de ses origines, mais celui d’une mémoire collective dont il a hérité sans l’avoir entièrement vécue. Il y a, dans cette démarche, quelque chose qui dépasse finalement la seule question afghane. Que signifie photographier un pays lorsque celui-ci existe déjà dans l’imaginaire du monde avant même que l’on déclenche son appareil ? « Afghanistan », un ouvrage de 240 pages paru au éditions teNeues/ Die Gestalten Verlag. #LeQuestionnaire #DanielMalikyar #CaroleSchmitz

Image 63: Documentary: A witness to the Belle Époque, World War I, the Roaring Twenties, the invention of aviation and the automobile… Jacques Henri Lartigue captured everything he experienced—and loved. A never-before-seen 3D journey into the photographer’s youth, in theaters across France on September 16. @jacqueshenri_lartigue @ufo.distribution Photo: Maurice Lartigue, surnommé Zissou, sur son « bob » à 4 roues, Rouzat, août 1910 vue gauche d’un positif stéréoscopique sur plaque de verre 8x16cm — — — — — Documentaire : Témoin de la Belle Époque, de la Première guerre mondiale, des Années folles, l’invention de l’aviation et de l’automobile… Jacques-Henri Lartigue captura tout ce qu'il traversa, et aima. Une plongée inédite en 3D relief dans la jeunesse du photographe, en salle partout en France le 16 septembre. #jacqueshenrilartigue

Image 67: Book: While his early shots explore the city with a dynamic eye, among crowded sidewalks and hidden corners, his more recent work addresses issues such as vulnerability and marginalization, never succumbing to the aestheticization of pain. 'A Closer Look' by Bruce Gilden is published by Skira. @bruce_gilden @skiraparis @magnumphotos Photo: Amber, Kensington, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA, 2023. © Bruce Gilden/Magnum Photos — — — — — Livre : Si ses premiers clichés explorent la ville d’un œil dynamique, entre trottoirs bondés et recoins cachés, ses travaux plus récents abordent des sujets tels que la vulnérabilité et la marginalisation, sans jamais céder à l’esthétisation de la douleur. 'A Closer Look' de Bruce Gilden est publié aux éditions Skira. #Skira #Photobook #BruceGilden

Image 69: Rencontres d'Arles 2026: Alam’s exhibition, Ozymandias (2020–ongoing), is an intimate and multidisciplinary body of work that examines memory, identity, and cognitive decline through the artist’s experience of caring for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. @alampanah @rencontresarles Photo: Ozymandias © Aman Alam — — — — — Rencontres d'Arles 2026 : L'exposition d'Alam, « Ozymandias » (2020–en cours), est un ensemble d'œuvres intimistes et multidisciplinaires qui explore la mémoire, l'identité et le déclin cognitif à travers l'expérience vécue par l'artiste lorsqu'il s'est occupé de sa grand-mère après qu'elle eut reçu un diagnostic de maladie d'Alzheimer. S'appuyant sur la photographie, la sculpture, l'intelligence artificielle et des archives familiales, ce projet explore ce que signifie se souvenir, oublier et prendre soin d'une personne dont le sentiment d'identité s'effrite progressivement. #arles #amanaman

Image 71: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 73: Book: Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Jo Ann Chaus, 'Unspoken' is published by Kehrer Verlag. @joann_chaus @kehrerverlag Photo: © Jo Ann Chaus / Kehrer Verlag — — — — — Livre : Jo Ann Chaus incarne une série de stéréotypes et d’archétypes féminins des figures façonnées par des attentes héritées et des rôles intériorisés. Bien qu’elle soit une femme moderne et indépendante, l’artiste a dû reconnaître à quel point elle demeurait encore attachée à la génération de sa mère, guidée par les idéaux de l’épouse dévouée et de la mère sacrifiée. 'Unspoken' est un livre publié aux éditions Kehrer Verlag. #joannchaud #kehrerverlag

Image 77: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 79: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Hiro and Avedon would go on to share a studio for the better part of two decades. This image of Hiro was photographed in Avedon’s apartment in 1990.” – The Richard Avedon Foundation

For its first exhibition devoted to still photography, Japan House London brings together two major figures of Japanese photography: Kawada Kikuji, born in 1933, and Iwane Ai, born in 1975. Titled Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai, the exhibition marks the two artists’ first joint presentation.

Born in 1933, Kawada Kikuji established himself in the 1960s as one of the most singular photographers of his generation. His body of work, at once prolific and shape-shifting, traces the transformations of postwar Japan and questions, across the decades, how the country has rebuilt and redefined its identity. In 1960, he took part in founding VIVO, a collective bringing together a number of young photographers eager to break with the conventions of their time. His work was notably shown at MoMA in New York in 1974. In 2011, the Photographic Society of Japan awarded him a prize honoring his entire career.

The London exhibition looks in particular at Chizu (The Map, 1965), a series that became one of the most important photobooks in Japanese history. In it, Kawada photographs the traces, scars, and signs left by the war, notably in Hiroshima, without seeking to describe them documentarily. In Los Caprichos (1968–1981), made up of urban snapshots, his gaze becomes more fragmentary and enigmatic. Together, these bodies of work mark a decisive break with earlier generations of Japanese photographers. The selection devoted to Kawada was curated by Sayaka Takahashi, of the PGI gallery in Tokyo.

Alongside him, Iwane Ai, born in Tokyo in 1975 and educated in the United States through high school, has developed a photography deeply shaped by displacement and stories of migration. Her work is often built between multiple territories and multiple memories. In Kipuka (2018), she turns to Japanese communities settled in Hawaii, in particular those whose roots trace back to Fukushima. Originally trained through magazine commissions, Iwane has since developed an award-winning body of work exhibited at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum, as well as in museums and galleries around the world.

With A New River (2020), Iwane traveled to the Tōhoku region during the Covid-19 pandemic. Cherry trees photographed at night stand alongside figures drawn from Japanese supernatural folklore. Between isolation, the fragility of the world, the passage of time, and hope, the series turns the landscape into a mental space where the present seems to converse with ancient stories. A New River is presented in London alongside Kipuka, as two variations on memory, belonging, and the ties that persist despite distance.

The exhibition is organized by the team of KYOTOGRAPHIE International Photography Festival, one of the most important photography festivals in Asia. Founded in 2013 by Lucille Reyboz and Nakanishi Yūsuke, every spring KYOTOGRAPHIE takes over Kyoto’s cultural venues — traditional houses, temples, galleries, and museums — turning the city into a vast territory devoted to photography. In 2025, the festival drew close to 300,000 visitors. Iwane was featured there in 2022, Kawada in 2024. Their reunion at Japan House London marks their first joint exhibition.

For Simon Wright, director of programming at Japan House, this exhibition represents “a great privilege”: “This is the first time Japan House London has devoted an exhibition to photography.” He highlights the two artists’ ability to address phenomena that concern us all. The exhibition is threaded through with stories of past and present that, on reflection, invite us to imagine our future together, whatever our origin.

Through Kawada and Iwane, Kyotographie thus brings into dialogue two generations and two ways of looking at Japan; one turned toward the wounds and upheavals of the postwar years, the other toward movement, migration, and contemporary forms of memory. A meeting between two temporalities, but also between two ways of making photographs, a place where the intimate meets history.

Jean-Jacques Ader

Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai Exhibition, 3 June to 18 October 2026 at Japan House London. Information:[**https://www.japanhouselondon.uk/**](https://www.japanhouselondon.uk/)

Published bySKIRA, Schiaparelli Anglomaniacexplores the creative dialogue between the House of Schiaparelli and a vibrant community of over 50 British artists, photographers, stylists, and image-makers. Edited by Thierry-Maxime Loriot and introduced by Dua Lipa, the book features a historical-critical essay by Loriot and a text by Robin Muir examining the historic collaborations between Schiaparelli and photographer Cecil Beaton.

The publication includes numerous previously unpublished images and artworks presented here for the first time, alongside interviews with Nick Knight, Stephen Jones, Dame Pat McGrath, Guido Palau, and Nadia Lee Cohen, with additional contributions by Trino Verkade.

Since Daniel Roseberry’s arrival at Schiaparelli, his singular creative vision has inspired a wide network of British talents across photography, illustration, performance, fashion editing, hair, and make-up. In the spirit of Elsa Schiaparelli’s original collaborations with artists, the book highlights the work of nearly fifty creatives spanning several generations.

Featured figures include historic photographers Cecil Beaton and Norman Parkinson; established artists such as Nick Knight, Tim Walker, and Pat McGrath; and a new generation including Nadine Ijewere, Campbell Addy, Felix Cooper, Nadia Lee Cohen, Jack Davison, Tom Craig, and Harley Weir. Together, these collaborators reflect the evolving cultural landscape surrounding the House.

Across disciplines and generations, these artists respond to the work of a single creative mind while asserting their own distinct perspectives. Their images and interventions reinterpret and subvert the established codes of both a fashion house and an industry, celebrating diversity, wit, and technical mastery.

Daniel Roseberry’s distinctive approach invites us into the dreamlike world shaped by the exquisite haute couture craftsmanship he has brought to the House. Rather than dwelling on the past, he propels Schiaparelli toward the future.

About the authors

Thierry-Maxime Loriotis a Canadian writer, curator, and creative director who has curated more than seventeen exhibitions dedicated to Jean Paul Gaultier worldwide, including in London, Paris, Melbourne, Buenos Aires, Munich, and Montreal. His internationally acclaimed touring exhibition The Fashion World of Jean Paul Gaultier: From the Sidewalk to the Catwalk was followed by Love is Love: Wedding Bliss for All à la Jean Paul Gaultier and Jean Paul Gaultier from A to Z for the France Pavilion at the Dubai World Expo in 2022. Loriot has also curated major touring exhibitions on Thierry Mugler and Viktor&Rolf and authored numerous books on fashion and photography. To date, his exhibitions have attracted more than six million visitors.

Robin Muiris a photographic historian, exhibition curator, and external curator for the National Portrait Gallery in London. A former picture editor at Vogue, he now serves as a contributing editor and consultant on its photographic archives. He has curated major exhibitions at the National Portrait Gallery, the Victoria and Albert Museum, and the Yale Center for British Art.

Trino Verkadeis director of the Sarabande Foundation. She worked closely with Alexander McQueen from the early years of his career, helping develop his business from a small creative studio into a global luxury brand. She also oversaw Savage Beauty, the landmark retrospective of McQueen’s work presented at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in 2011.

The MIT Press publishes Tumbados :Lowriding Memories and Cruising Futuresedited by Guadalupe Rosales. A candid and timely celebration of lowrider culture that examines the politics of cruising, the Latinx experience, and the artwork of Guadalupe Rosales.

Tumbados, or lowriders, are customized, intricately painted cars with a dropped suspension that pay tribute to Chicano pride, artistry, culture, and heritage. Originating in Southern California in the 1940s, lowriders are a vibrant symbol of Latinx street life and the politics of cruising—a term that refers to the cars parading slowly down streets. After a period of public rejection in the 1980s and 90s, lowriders gained recognition as an important form of cultural expression and as an art form.

In Tumbados, artist Guadalupe Rosales and her national network of collaborators explore art, craft, collective memory, and displacement through the lens of Latinx and diasporic experience. The book contextualizes Rosales’ major public mural commission on lowriders with Lokey Calderon, commissioned by the Storefront for Art and Architecture, while tracing cultural narratives of marginalization and resilience across bodies, objects, walls, and public space.

Though lowriders are celebrated in popular culture, little is understood about their social and historic significance. This will be the first book to examine Rosales’ comprehensive practice, known for fostering collective storytelling, and to surface a subject often overlooked in the public record and in official memory.

Danziger Gallery presents an online exhibition of Julian Wasser’s photographs ofJoan Didion– a remembrance of two great artists linked through one photographic assignment.

Made in Los Angeles in 1968, at a moment when the young writer was emerging as one of the most distinctive voices in American literature,TIME Magazine assigned Wasser to photograph Didion at her rented house on Franklin Avenue in Hollywood. Her collection “Slouching Towards Bethlehem” was becoming a literary sensation, confirming her place as a writer of exceptional precision and an acute observer of the shifting social landscape of California.

Wasser began his career in photography in the Washington, D.C. bureau of the Associated Press, where he met and accompanied the legendary news photographer Weegee, who would become an important and lasting influence. By the mid-1960s, Wasser had moved to Los Angeles, working as a contract photographer for TIME,LIFE, and FORTUNE. There he established a reputation for an unusual combination of access and intuition: an ability to enter the private worlds of his subjects and make photographs that appeared spontaneous while remaining remarkably assured in their composition.

With regard to Didion,“I’d read her fiction,” Wasser recalled, “and she didn’t miss a thing. She was a heavyweight.”The photographs began inside the house before Wasser and Didion moved outdoors, where he photographed her with her recently acquired yellow Corvette Stingray. Didion appears variously as writer, mother, and newly minted California icon. Seated quietly inside her house; holding her daughter Quintana Roo on her lap; or framed by the sleek geometry of the Corvette,Wasser’s photographs seem to contain many of the contradictions that would become associated with Didion herself—the private and the public, fragility and authority, glamour and detachment.

Didion would later identify the portrait with Quintana Roo as her favorite. Yet it was Wasser’s photographs of her with the Corvette, together with the indoor three-quarter portrait, that have become especially influential style images. Their visual language has continued to reverberate through popular culture, notably in a later Celine campaign in which a model was posed in the window of a car directly referencing Wasser’s portrait of Didion.(To Celine’s credit, shortly afterward they convinced Didion to pose in her own Celine ad wearing chic oversize sunglasses.)

Viewed today, more than half a century after they were made, Wasser’s photographs are striking not simply because of the cultural stature Didion would attain, but because of Wasser’s instinct for the revealing moment. There is remarkably little theatricality in them. Their authority comes instead from proximity, observation, and an apparent absence of effort.In doing so Wasser would create some of the most enduring portraits of an American writer.

Julian Wasser : Joan Didion. “Remembering”Online exhibition

952 5th Ave #2D

New York, NY 10075

Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. @alampanah @rencontresarles Photo: Ozymandias © Aman Alam — — — — — Rencontres d'Arles 2026 : L'exposition d'Alam, « Ozymandias » (2020–en cours), est un ensemble d'œuvres intimistes et multidisciplinaires qui explore la mémoire, l'identité et le déclin cognitif à travers l'expérience vécue par l'artiste lorsqu'il s'est occupé de sa grand-mère après qu'elle eut reçu un diagnostic de maladie d'Alzheimer. S'appuyant sur la photographie, la sculpture, l'intelligence artificielle et des archives familiales, ce projet explore ce que signifie se souvenir, oublier et prendre soin d'une personne dont le sentiment d'identité s'effrite progressivement. #arles #amanaman

Image 77: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 79: Book: Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Jo Ann Chaus, 'Unspoken' is published by Kehrer Verlag. @joann_chaus @kehrerverlag Photo: © Jo Ann Chaus / Kehrer Verlag — — — — — Livre : Jo Ann Chaus incarne une série de stéréotypes et d’archétypes féminins des figures façonnées par des attentes héritées et des rôles intériorisés. Bien qu’elle soit une femme moderne et indépendante, l’artiste a dû reconnaître à quel point elle demeurait encore attachée à la génération de sa mère, guidée par les idéaux de l’épouse dévouée et de la mère sacrifiée. 'Unspoken' est un livre publié aux éditions Kehrer Verlag. #joannchaud #kehrerverlag

Image 83: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 85: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 87: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 89: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

Archives – August 21, 2020

After the financial crisis of the 1970’s decimated New York City’s public programs and infrastructure, the subway in particular was arguably at its nadir in terms of maintenance, upkeep, and crime as the decade came to a close. It was precisely at this moment, however, that Bruce Davidson began photographing it in a sustained and systematic way. The subway he traversed then, from the Bronx down to Coney Island and Rockaway Beach, seems a distant image from the one we ride today. Howard Greenberg and Bruce Davidson sat down recently over Zoom to discuss Davidson’s now-classic project “Subway”.

The following conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Howard Greenberg: Bruce Davidson is not only one of the great photographers of the 20th century, he’s different than the others as well. He made his mark in the field early on as a young man by creating an extended photo essay on a Brooklyn street gang called the Jokers. Today we’re going to talk mostly about his work on the New York City subway. (Subway was first published by Aperture in 1986).

These days, where color photography has really emerged as the primary medium for art photography, Subway stands as protype of what was to come. The subway was a subject for you to explore and photograph and make this incredible essay around 1980. What led you to it? Especially at such a dangerous time in New York City?

Bruce Davidson: I still haven’t come to terms with what it means. I think I’m still attached to it in a certain way though. It’s important that there’s a meaning to my photographs, a passion that sustains me, and a clear reason for being there. In 1979/1980 the subway contained all those things for me. Though in its own way, it was as desolate as a body of work could be.

It was dark; I used a flash to signal that there was an event taking place in the subway. Subway is about aspiration. I fastened myself as a hunter would.

HG: By using the flash purposefully, you were really calling attention to yourself. You became the event. It was courageous to do something like that.

BD: The flash wasn’t always there, particularly if it felt too dangerous. But it helped me explore color, passion, and meaning.

I think that beauty was and still is a possibility in the subway. I met remarkable people over that period of 3 or 4 years. One woman was standing on the platform and her dress was blowing in the wind. I didn’t want to frighten her, so I went up to her and asked permission. She became one of my favorite encounters in this body of work.

HG: You’ve shown me some black and white work that you did on the subway, yet most people only know the color work. Why is that, and how did that all go down?

BD: Well it began in black and white because that’s who I thought I was, but I also saw that there was something else happening in the subway that had to do with color. Although I prefer the black and white – there are only about two dozen images – they were the old Bruce Davidson. I felt this project had more meaning in color.

HG: You made the right choice as far I’m concerned.

I’ll digress a little bit. Although I knew your work before we started to work together, I’ve grown to know it more deeply since you joined the gallery over twenty years ago, and I have the most enormous respect for how you’ve approached making photographs and how you’ve gone about making your creative choices.

BD: Thank you. My wife has made me see that the facts of someone’s life are more important than my artistic expression.

HG: I think that’s what makes your photographs so impactful.

How did it work with the people you were photographing in the subway. You were close to some of them. What was that interaction like?

BD: There have been times after the fact that I’ve sent a little print to the person in the photograph. I carried a little album to show people my work. There’s a picture of a young man with a scar on his face, and I looked into the camera and he said, “Don’t take my picture or I’ll break your camera.” And I said, “No no, I would never without your permission” – which was a lie. So I showed him my album, and he let me photograph him.

When you come to the end of the book, though, the pictures become more abstracted.

HG: The only reason the work could expand and change and evolve and become more abstract is the commitment to doing this project for a long period of time.

BD: I’m glad you understand and support the work.

HG: It’s been my great pleasure.

Archives – August 21, 2023

Michael Benson : Passion Photo.

Michael Benson began his career in higher education. He joined the London Institute (now University of the Arts, London) in 1993. There he led a successful national campaign to secure a major new site for Chelsea College of Arts. He also directed the Insitute Gallery, organizing over 50 exhibitions. “Signatures of the invisible”, his collaboration with CERN (Geneva), led to a world tour of exhibitions that ended at PS1Moma in 2003. Two months later, he left his job to create Candlestar with Fariba Farshad. A duo for whom nothing seems to stand in the way.

Experts in the conception, design and production of ambitious cultural projects, the agency specializes in photography.

Over the past twenty years, Candlestar has become synonymous with the development of world-class cultural events, including Frieze, Art Dubai and the Condé Nast College of Fashion.

Since its creation fifteen years ago, Candlestar has produced over 120 Prix Pictet exhibitions in museums around the world.

Michael Benson is also the founding director of the Prix Pictet (created in 2008), the most important award for photography and sustainable development.

In 2015, the agency created “Photo London”, an internationally renowned annual event that took up residence in London’s iconic Somerset House. The growing number of exhibitors, the continuing development of the London audience and the array of satellite events held across the city during the event have all contributed to making Photo London a very special event.

Michael Benson has also written and edited over twenty books, including fourteen for the Prix Pictet.

His “1000 words 1000 years” (Camberwell Press) won the prestigious D&D Yellow Pencil in 2000.

More recently, Michael has written two books to support the annual exhibition program of the Marta Ortega Perez Foundation (MOP), based in La Coruña. Raw Beauty, his book on Peter Lindbergh, was published in 2021 and the one on Steven Meisel in 2022, with whom he also conducted interviews published in Vogue and Modern Weekly (Shanghai).

This year, Candlestar is teaming up with Creo/Montgomery Arts to launch a new photography event to be held at New York’s Javits Centre in September, PHOTOFAIRS New York.

Stay tuned!

Website : www.candlestar.co.uk

Your first photographic trigger ?Michael Benson : There were two. First PH Emerson’ Reed Cutters (lived for a while in a mid-Norfolk that hasn’t changed much since Emerson’ time) and then later Don McCullin’s 1970 image of a homeless Irishman .

The man or woman of image who inspires you ?Michael Benson : Photographers -too many to name just one – Lindbergh, Meisel, McCullin, Salgado, Diane Arbus, Graciela Iturbide, Newsha Tavakolian, Shirin Neshat… Outside that Marta Ortega Pérez and Maja Hoffmann are simply remarkable…

The image you would have liked to make ?Michael Benson : Lightning Fields by Hiroshi Sugimoto.

The one that moved you the most ?Michael Benson : Peter Lindbergh’s handwritten lament for his friend Pina Bausch on his 1997 image Atelier Baude.

And the one that made you angry ?Michael Benson : The image of our fuckwit former Prime Minister in front of his £350 million Brexit battle bus -endlessly infuriating.

A key image in your personal pantheon ?Michael Benson : Pick any image from Benoit Acquin’s ‘Chinese Dustbowl’ series which won the very first Prix Pictet in 2008. We didn’t know it at the time but 120 exhibitions and ten editions later it was clearly the start of something big…

A photographic memory from your childhood ?Michael Benson : 1966. Nobby Stiles dancing with the World Cup in one hand and his dentures in the other.

With no budget limit, what would be the work you would dream of acquiring ?Michael Benson : Either Sappho by Julia Margaret Cameron, Beckett by Avedon or a Lebensmittel grid by Michael Schmidt along with the cash to build somewhere big enough to house it.

According to you, what is the necessary quality to be a good photographer ?Michael Benson : Obsession with what you are doing almost to exclusion of everything else. After that its down to timing and light.

The secret of the perfect image, if it exists ?Michael Benson : No secrets. Just hard work and a bit of magic.

The person you would like to photograph ?Michael Benson : Steven Meisel or Didier Drogba.

An indispensable photo book ?Michael Benson : A subject of endless debate here at Candlestar towers Not a book per se but Larry Schaaf’s stunning Fox Talbot Catalogue Raisonné project is as close to indispensable as it gets…

The camera of your childhood ?Michael Benson : An Instamatic that I traded for a Curved Air picture disk.

The one you use today ?Michael Benson : An antique Nikon. My iphone and a telescope with which I take pictures of the stars.

Your favorite drug ?Michael Benson : Alcohol. Anything made at Chateau La Calisse just outside Barjols in la Provence Verte, to be precise.

The best way to disconnect for you ?Michael Benson : Friday night. My chilling on my terrace in Cotignac at sunset in one of our Martin Parr deckchairs. Good company. Music. Great wine…

What is your relationship with the image ?Michael Benson : Tricky. Troublesome. Too often awestruck.

Your greatest quality ?Michael Benson : Self-irony.

Your latest folly?Michael Benson : 2022/23 Chelsea season ticket … Things can only get better.

An image to illustrate a new banknote?Michael Benson : Buck Moon.

The job you would not have liked to do ?Michael Benson : I spent one winter in a freezing cellar splitting pigs and preparing Turkeys for Christmas. Never ever again…

Your greatest professional extravagance?Michael Benson : Two Italian handmade desks that we bought on the day we set up Candlestar. They were almost too big to fit into our shoe box of an office. It took us years to pay for them.

The city, the country or the culture you dream of discovering ?Michael Benson : I am woefully ill travelled in Latin America and Africa. I dream of Tierra del Fuego and Accra…

The place you never get tired of ?Michael Benson : Two. London and Cotignac.

Your biggest regret ?Michael Benson : Two again. Not starting Candlestar ten years earlier than we did. John Terry’s European Cup Final penalty miss against Manchester United…

In terms of social networks, are you more into Instagram, Facebook, Tik Tok or Snapchat and why ?Michael Benson : None of them. For business they are an absolutely necessary evil but personally I’d rather chew of my own arm than sign up for any of them.

Color or B&W ?Michael Benson : Both.

Daylight or artificial light ?Michael Benson : Daylight.

Which city do you think is the most photogenic ?Michael Benson : Mexico City.

If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you opt for a selfie with him ?Michael Benson : It’s a big ‘if’ but if he wants to pop round, we could see what materialises.

If I could organize your ideal dinner party, who would be at the table ?Michael Benson : Samuel Beckett, Sally Mann, Didier Drogba, Fox Talbot, Rimbaud, Peter Lindbergh, Joni Mitchell, Azzedine Alaïa and my wife, Fariba, who enjoys this kind of thing…

The image that represents for you the current state of the world ?Michael Benson : I see an awful lot of these for the Prix Pictet but right now Ragnar Axelson’s 2016 Series ‘Where the World is Melting’ is a pretty good statement of the mess we are in…

What is missing in today’s world ?Michael Benson : A sense of humour.

If you had to start all over again ?Michael Benson : I’d start from here.

A last word ?Michael Benson :That night in the desert the stars were close as candles….

Diogenes

This series does not seek to explain a pathology, nor to act as a witness or prosecutor of a situation. It is simply a matter of photographing this theme like any other subject, without hierarchy or judgement. The exclusive use of the 50mm lens allows for a restricted frame that faithfully reflects the reality of the place: it does not seek to open up the horizon, but rather exposes the enclosed space, the withdrawal, and the invisible confinement within which a life has taken root.

​The aim is to photograph in a raw, unadorned manner, without artifice or staging. By focusing on fragments and on the poetry of juxtaposed objects, these photographs refrain from cataloguing or mapping out squalor.

​The sole intention is to uphold the dignity of the individual by capturing their world with an accurate gaze.

The photography seeks to offer a breath of fresh air: that of not imprisoning this existence a second time.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/fra.content:
Imaginarium (botanical fantasy)

Since the dawn of time, humankind has sought to bend nature to its will in order to mould it in its own image.

Through these photographs, I reimagine the plant world by removing it from its original environment – not to adapt it to our human perspective, but rather to amplify its power and perceive its beauty to the fullest.

I enjoy taking the time to collect fragments of flowers or plants, and to create compositions from them that spring from my imagination.

Reconstructing these flowers whilst respecting their essence fosters a collective awareness of each of these small things that surround us.

It seems to me essential, even more so today, to slow down in order to perceive the beauty of nature and, in doing so, to respect it.

Image 56: Book: Published by SKIRA, 'Schiaparelli Anglomaniac' explores the creative dialogue between the House of Schiaparelli and a vibrant community of over 50 British artists, photographers, stylists, and image-makers. The book is edited by Thierry-Maxime Loriot and introduced by Dua Lipa. @nadineijewere @schiaparelli @thierrymaximeloriot @dualipa Photo: Nadine Ijewere, Divine Mugisha, Luncheon, 2023. Spring/Summer 2023 ‘Inferno’ HC collection, look #19 Instagram @nadineijewere © Nadine Ijewere — — — — — Livre : Publié par SKIRA, 'Schiaparelli Anglomaniac' explore le dialogue créatif entre la maison Schiaparelli et une communauté vivante de plus de 50 artistes, photographes, stylistes et créateurs d’images britanniques. Le livre est édité par Thierry-Maxime Loriot, avec une préface de Dua Lipa. #photobook #skira #fashion #britishfashion #schiaparelli

Image 58: Exhibition: In 'Los Caprichos' (1968–1981), made up of urban snapshots, Kawada Kikuji's gaze becomes more fragmentary and enigmatic. Together, these bodies of work mark a decisive break with earlier generations of Japanese photographers. On view at Japan House, part of the dialogue 'Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai'. @kawada_kikuji @ai_iwane_studio @kyotographie @japanhouseldn @tkhs_sayaka Photo: Kikuji Kawada From the series 'Los Caprichos' Invisible © Kikuji Kawada — — — — — Exposition : Dans « Los Caprichos » (1968-1981), une série composée d’instantanés urbains, le regard de Kawada Kikuji se fait plus fragmentaire et énigmatique. Ensemble, ces séries marquent une rupture décisive avec les générations précédentes de photographes japonais. Exposition présentée à la Japan House, dans le cadre du dialogue « Kyotographie : Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai ». #japanhouse #kyotographie #kawadakikuji #iwaneai

Image 60: Exhibition: Here is Ruth’s recipe for a long and happy life. Never get used to anything Hold on to the child within you Keep your curiosity alive Trust your intuition Enjoy the simple things Say ‘yes’ to life with passion Fall madly in love with the world Don’t forget: today is the day ~ Ruth Bernhard, October 14, 1995 On view at Peter Fetterman. @peterfettermangallery Photo: Ruth Bernhard (1905-2006) - Hips Horizontal, 1975 © Trustees of Princeton University - Courtesy of Peter Fetterman Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Voici la recette de Ruth de Bernhard pour une vie longue et heureuse. Ne t’habitue jamais à rien Garde en toi l’enfant qui sommeille en toi Entretiens ta curiosité Fais confiance à ton intuition Apprécie les petites choses de la vie Dis « oui » à la vie avec passion Tombe follement amoureux du monde N’oublie pas : c’est aujourd’hui qu’il faut vivre pleinement ~ Ruth Bernhard 14 octobre 1995 À voir à la Peter Fetterman Gallery.

Image 62: Exhibition: In her very first exhibition in France, Erjola Zhuka depicts everyday scenes and raw moments with her friends and family, imbued with a powerful sense of reality and spontaneity. The exhibition is titled 'MyTh-ing' carrying a double meaning, referring to both “myth” and “my thing”. “For me, myth is these people (that appear in the images).” On view at IRIS Arles until October 4. @iris_arles @erjola_zhuka Photo: © Erjola Zhuka — — — — — Exposition : Pour sa première exposition en France, Erjola Zhuka dépeint des scènes du quotidien et des instants bruts passés avec ses amis, empreints d’un puissant sentiment de réalité et de spontanéité. Le titre MyTh-ing revêt un double sens, faisant référence à la fois au « mythe » et à « ma chose » ; l’artiste explique : « Pour moi, le mythe, ce sont ces personnes (qui apparaissent dans les images). » #irisarles #erjolazhuka

Image 64: Exhibition: North Korea is one of the most closed dictatorships in the world. Stéphan Gladieu traveled there five times to create a series of portraits between 2017 and 2020. Duly authorized to enter this country of absolute control, and accompanied at all times, he used his mobile photography studio to recreate a space of freedom, playing with backdrops and the visual codes of propaganda. @stephangladieu @musee_des_confluences Photo: North Koreans Portraits North Korea PyongYang June 2018 Kim Yun Gyong, Han Sol Gyong, Kim Won Gyong, Kang Sun Hwa and Kong Su Hyang in the 3D movie theater at SCI Tech Complex. © Stéphan Gladieu - Courtesy Musée des Confluences — — — — — Exposition : La Corée du Nord est l’une des dictatures les plus fermées au monde. Stéphan Gladieu s’y est rendu à cinq reprises pour réaliser une série de portraits entre 2017 et 2020. Ayant obtenu l’autorisation nécessaire pour entrer dans ce pays soumis à un contrôle absolu, et accompagné en permanence, il a utilisé son studio de photographie mobile pour recréer un espace de liberté, en jouant avec les arrière-plans et les codes visuels de la propagande. #stephanegladieu #museedesconfluences #northkorea

Image 66: Exhibition: The Photography+ Emerging Talent returns for its second edition. With more than 1300 submissions from across the world, this initiative still builds on the simple idea that started it: talent does not only come with a qualification. This issue features the work of Lèa Chen (TW/UK), Tamás Cseke (HU), Angus Fayers (UK), Joel Jimenez Jara (CR), Grace Tenneh Kromah (US), Grace Martella (IT), Alice Poyzer (UK), Paula Elena Ramos (ES), Diana Sosnowska (IT/PL/US), Farhad Yasavoli (IR/UK). @takenbyleachen @photoworks_uk Photo: Longing for the Spring Breeze 2026 © Léa Chen — — — — Exposition : Le concours « Photography+ Emerging Talent » revient pour sa deuxième édition. Avec plus de 1 300 candidatures venues du monde entier, cette initiative reste fidèle à l’idée simple qui est à l’origine de sa création : le talent ne se résume pas à un diplôme. Ce numéro présente les travaux de Lèa Chen (Taïwan/Royaume-Uni), Tamás Cseke (Hongrie), Angus Fayers (Royaume-Uni), Joel Jimenez Jara (CR), Grace Tenneh Kromah (US), Grace Martella (IT), Alice Poyzer (UK), Paula Elena Ramos (ES), Diana Sosnowska (IT/PL/US) et Farhad Yasavoli (IR/UK).

Image 68: The Questionnaire: With Afghanistan, his most personal project to date, Daniel Malikyar undertakes a form of visual reclamation. He photographs a country that is not only the land of his origins, but also the bearer of a collective memory he inherited without ever having fully experienced it. There is, ultimately, something in this approach that extends beyond the Afghan questions alone. What does it mean to photograph a country when it already exists in the world’s imagination before the shutter is even released? Afghanistan, a 240-page book published by teNeues / Die Gestalten Verlag. @dmalikyar ✍️ A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: © Daniel Malikyar - Courtesy teNeues — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Avec Afghanistan, son projet le plus personnel, Daniel Malikyar entreprend alors une forme de reconquête visuelle. Il photographie un pays qui n’est pas seulement celui de ses origines, mais celui d’une mémoire collective dont il a hérité sans l’avoir entièrement vécue. Il y a, dans cette démarche, quelque chose qui dépasse finalement la seule question afghane. Que signifie photographier un pays lorsque celui-ci existe déjà dans l’imaginaire du monde avant même que l’on déclenche son appareil ? « Afghanistan », un ouvrage de 240 pages paru au éditions teNeues/ Die Gestalten Verlag. #LeQuestionnaire #DanielMalikyar #CaroleSchmitz

Image 70: Documentary: A witness to the Belle Époque, World War I, the Roaring Twenties, the invention of aviation and the automobile… Jacques Henri Lartigue captured everything he experienced—and loved. A never-before-seen 3D journey into the photographer’s youth, in theaters across France on September 16. @jacqueshenri_lartigue @ufo.distribution Photo: Maurice Lartigue, surnommé Zissou, sur son « bob » à 4 roues, Rouzat, août 1910 vue gauche d’un positif stéréoscopique sur plaque de verre 8x16cm — — — — — Documentaire : Témoin de la Belle Époque, de la Première guerre mondiale, des Années folles, l’invention de l’aviation et de l’automobile… Jacques-Henri Lartigue captura tout ce qu'il traversa, et aima. Une plongée inédite en 3D relief dans la jeunesse du photographe, en salle partout en France le 16 septembre. #jacqueshenrilartigue

Image 74: Book: While his early shots explore the city with a dynamic eye, among crowded sidewalks and hidden corners, his more recent work addresses issues such as vulnerability and marginalization, never succumbing to the aestheticization of pain. 'A Closer Look' by Bruce Gilden is published by Skira. @bruce_gilden @skiraparis @magnumphotos Photo: Amber, Kensington, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA, 2023. © Bruce Gilden/Magnum Photos — — — — — Livre : Si ses premiers clichés explorent la ville d’un œil dynamique, entre trottoirs bondés et recoins cachés, ses travaux plus récents abordent des sujets tels que la vulnérabilité et la marginalisation, sans jamais céder à l’esthétisation de la douleur. 'A Closer Look' de Bruce Gilden est publié aux éditions Skira. #Skira #Photobook #BruceGilden

Image 76: Rencontres d'Arles 2026: Alam’s exhibition, Ozymandias (2020–ongoing), is an intimate and multidisciplinary body of work that examines memory, identity, and cognitive decline through the artist’s experience of caring for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. @alampanah @rencontresarles Photo: Ozymandias © Aman Alam — — — — — Rencontres d'Arles 2026 : L'exposition d'Alam, « Ozymandias » (2020–en cours), est un ensemble d'œuvres intimistes et multidisciplinaires qui explore la mémoire, l'identité et le déclin cognitif à travers l'expérience vécue par l'artiste lorsqu'il s'est occupé de sa grand-mère après qu'elle eut reçu un diagnostic de maladie d'Alzheimer. S'appuyant sur la photographie, la sculpture, l'intelligence artificielle et des archives familiales, ce projet explore ce que signifie se souvenir, oublier et prendre soin d'une personne dont le sentiment d'identité s'effrite progressivement. #arles #amanaman

Image 78: Exhibition: Peter Hujar was a central figure in the queer downtown scene in New York in the 1970s and early 1980s. When he died of AIDS-related pneumonia in 1987, his photographs were largely unknown to the wider art world. With his classically composed black-and-white photographs — portraits, animals, architecture and landscapes, mostly focused on a single subject explored in its full presence — Peter Hujar stood apart from the photographic currents of his time. On view at the Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn. @peterhujarfoundation @bundeskunsthalle Photo: Peter Hujar, Gary Schneider Contortion (II), 1979 © The Peter Hujar Archive / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2026, Courtesy of The Peter Hujar Archive / ARS, New York, and Pace Gallery, Fraenkel Gallery, Maureen Paley, and Mai36 — — — — — Exposition : Le photographe Peter Hujar fut une figure centrale de la scène queer du downtown new-yorkais des années 1970 et du début des années 1980. Lorsqu’il meurt d’une pneumonie liée au sida en 1987, ses photographies restent largement méconnues du monde de l’art. Avec ses photographies en noir et blanc d’inspiration classique — portraits, animaux, architecture et paysages, le plus souvent centrés sur un sujet unique qu’il explore dans toute sa présence — Peter Hujar se distingue des courants photographiques de son époque. #peterhujar #bundeskunsthalle

Image 80: Book: Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Jo Ann Chaus, 'Unspoken' is published by Kehrer Verlag. @joann_chaus @kehrerverlag Photo: © Jo Ann Chaus / Kehrer Verlag — — — — — Livre : Jo Ann Chaus incarne une série de stéréotypes et d’archétypes féminins des figures façonnées par des attentes héritées et des rôles intériorisés. Bien qu’elle soit une femme moderne et indépendante, l’artiste a dû reconnaître à quel point elle demeurait encore attachée à la génération de sa mère, guidée par les idéaux de l’épouse dévouée et de la mère sacrifiée. 'Unspoken' est un livre publié aux éditions Kehrer Verlag. #joannchaud #kehrerverlag

Image 84: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 86: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/cha.content:
A View on Flowers

Flowers pull me into their aura. Like butterflies and bees. When the sun shines through their petals, I am mesmerised by their colors. Absorbing and reflecting the light. Endless variety of form, surface of their leaves, undulations, indentations, iterations, thorns, stamen and ovary.

Focussed on their beauty, I circle around, kneel to compose a memory. To reflect.

Life knows no straight lines, no clear path, no goal other than to reproduce, to continue the lines, regenerate, co-exist.

Flowers wither, turn into fruits. Seeds are dispersed. And next spring they revive.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/mic.content:
Trees and stones form two complementary facets of the landscape: one living, breathing, changing with the seasons; the other mineral, silent, bearing witness to geological time.

Trees connect the sky and the earth, harbour biodiversity and tell the story of climates and humankind.

Stones, for their part, hold the deep memory of the earth—strata, fossils, mineral veins—and serve as foundations for human settlements.

Together, they form a dialectic of permanence and metamorphosis: roots cracking the rock, rain sculpting the cliffs, lichens transforming surfaces.

Understanding their interaction means grasping the dynamics of the living and the non-living, and putting our place in a timescale stretching across centuries and millennia into perspective.

The use of black and white can create a timeless and dramatic atmosphere, emphasising the solitude and immensity of the landscape. This artistic choice highlights the contrasts and textures of the desert terrain.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/sit.content:
The streets of Istanbul is full of surprises and hidden art. as stated by John Freely below…

“This is my Istanbul”

“No city has eaten the fruits of the garden of art so richly as the city of Istanbul, birthplace and school of famous men, the nursery of many nations.”

Nabî

I approach Istanbul today as I did when I first saw the city more than half a lifetime ago, taking a ferry from a suburban village on the Bosporus, the incomparably beautiful strait that divides Europe from Asia. On the way, I pass beneath two bridges that link the European and Asian sides of Istanbul, the only city in the world that spans two continents.

Between the scimitar-shaped inlet of the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara is the old city of Stamboul, known first as Byzantium and later as Constantinople – after its celebrated emperor. The chronicler Procopius more than 13 centuries ago described the city, its seven hills today crowned with the monuments of two world empires, as being “surrounded by a garland of waters.” As the ferry approaches its berth, I can see the former Byzantine cathedral of Hagia Sofia on the First Hill and the Süleymaniye Mosque dominating the Fourth Hill—imposing edifices erected a thousand years apart.

Stepping ashore, I find myself at the epicenter of all the city’s tumultuous life, the quay thronged with shoppers from the Spice Bazaar and the street markets around Yeni Cami (called the New Mosque because it was founded only four centuries ago). Fish sandwiches are sold from boats. Loudspeakers blare the latest songs. Peddlers sell sunglasses on bright summer days and umbrellas when it pours—when stovepipes are hawked, we know winter is near.

Midway through the 27th century of its turbulent existence, the city has survived sieges, sacks, conquests, civil wars, riots, plagues, fires, earthquakes, and the modern construction necessitated by a population that’s mushroomed from less than a million to more than ten million in 83 years. It has retained its identity through successive changes of name, population, language, religion, and political status, its character and spirit enduring through the centuries as if it had an ageless soul. As the French traveler Petrus Gyllius remarked in the mid-16th century: “It seems to me that while other cities are mortal, this one will endure as long as there are men on Earth.”

Diogenes

This series does not seek to explain a pathology, nor to act as a witness or prosecutor of a situation. It is simply a matter of photographing this theme like any other subject, without hierarchy or judgement. The exclusive use of the 50mm lens allows for a restricted frame that faithfully reflects the reality of the place: it does not seek to open up the horizon, but rather exposes the enclosed space, the withdrawal, and the invisible confinement within which a life has taken root.

​The aim is to photograph in a raw, unadorned manner, without artifice or staging. By focusing on fragments and on the poetry of juxtaposed objects, these photographs refrain from cataloguing or mapping out squalor.

​The sole intention is to uphold the dignity of the individual by capturing their world with an accurate gaze.

The photography seeks to offer a breath of fresh air: that of not imprisoning this existence a second time.
